How many officers and men are permanently employed in positions which are non-combatant, in connection with the Overseas Militia Department in London, England?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: None of the officers and men employed in London, England are permanent except those that have been seconded from the permanent staff and permanent force of the Canadian active militia. All of them, except those that belong to non-combatant units in the military sense, such as Canadian Army Pay Corps and Canadian Ordnance Corps, are combatant.

With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the Minister of Militia to the fact that the answer he has given is an evasion of the question. I should like my hon. friend at a later date to answer my question by stating how many officers and men have been sent over from the permanent staff and permanent force to perform the duties to which I refeT. As to the minister's reference to the fact that those who belong to non-combatant units in the military sense are combatants, I would point out that I was referring to the noncombatant positions, not to the men themselves. My hon. friend's answer, therefore, is not an answer at all, and I should like an assurance that later he will give me the information for which I asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There was no intention whatever to evade the question put by the member for Pictou. His question clearly is:
How many officers and men are permanently employed in positions which are non-combatant?	i
The word "permanently" is understood to mean permanently as opposed to temporarily; the word has the same effect in the camps in England as it has in Canada. Men who are non-combatant in a military sense are men who belong to the Army Pay Corps, the Ordnance Corps and units of that kind. Does my hon. friend refer to those who are occupying positions of a civilian character? If he will be good

enough to put his question in some way so that the information sought will be clearly defined, we will try to answer it.

The men who are employed in connection with the Overseas Militia Department are certainly non-combatants while they are so employed, no matter what corps they are attached to. In his answer my hon. friend excepted those men with reference to whom information should have been given. I will put the question in another way, and I hope I shall receive the information that I am seeking.

COAL SUPPLIES IN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON THE COAL SITUATION.
speechtext: I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if be will give us a report with regard to the coal situation. He said yesterday that he would do so to-day.

subtopic: COAL SUPPLIES IN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON THE COAL SITUATION.
speechtext:
I can give a very general statement in reference to the coal situation, which, if it has not been followed closely by the members of the House may not be within their knowledge. The coal situation in Canada, as it presents itself, is about as follows: The production last year of non-anthracite coals in Canada amounted to 13,800,000 tons. Of that production a little over 6,000,000 tons came from the Maritime Provinces (Nova Scotia almost entirely); 2,800,000 tons was raised in British Columbia, 4,600,000 tons in Alberta, and a small proportion in Saskatchewan, making altogether the amount raised about 13,800,000 tons. That, however, was

not sufficient for the needs of Canada, and in addition to that about 13,000,000 tons of bituminous coal had to be imported from the United States. Of the importation of bituminous coal, about 2,500,000 tons went to Quebec, 5,500,000 tons to central Ontario, 5,000,000 tons to the Georgian Bay and lake ports. The importation of 13,000,000 tons and the amount raised in Canada of 13,000,000 tons represent our available supplies for consumption after deducting about 1,800,000 tons, which was exported for bunkerage and other purposes, and some little which was exported to the United States. That is the situation in reference to the bituminous part of the coal business.
As regards anthracite, we are dependent for our supplies under present circumstances on the United States. Last year 4,500,000 tons of anthracite were imported^ into Canada. About one-quarter of a million tons went to the Maritime Provinces, a little over 1,000,000 tons went to Quebec, a little over 2,000,000 tons to Ontario and a small proportion-half a million tons or so-to Manitoba and the near west provinces. In addition to the bituminous coal amounting to 13,000,000 tons imported therefore, we imported anthracite coal to the amount of 4,500,000 tons, making a total importation of fuel coal for domestic and industrial purposes of 17,500,000 tons.
Anthracite stocks in this country were pretty well lowered last year, or at the end of the last coal year, and probably
1.000.	000 tons extra will have to be imported of anthracite in order to make up for the deficiency, which means that we are dependent upon the United States for about
18.000.	000 tons of coal.
With reference to our own production of coal, there is not any possibility that I can see that the amount raised this year will be in excess of the amount raised last year. In the West there have been coal strikes, and consequent delays and confusion, which have reduced to that extent the possible output. In Nova Scotia the shortage of labour, owing to enlistments and other causes, has been so great that it has been impossible for them to add to the production this year. On the other hand, the consumption demand in the Maritime Provinces' has increased and the situation in that respect is that what is raised in the Maritime Provinces will not be more than sufficient to take care of the needs or demands of the Maritime Provinces. What formerly came to Quebec (quite a large proportion of it from the 303jr
bituminous output of Nova Scotia) will have now to be supplied by imports from the United States.
That is the situation in so far as Canada is concerned and therefore the situation in the United States becomes of more interest to us. What then, in its brief and broad features, is the situation in the United States? The normal output of anthracite coal in the United States is between
67,000,000 and 68,000,000 tons-last year it was 67,700,000. The output of commercial bituminous coal in the United States, sold on the market, last year was 509,000,000 tons. The beginning of the coal year, the first of April, had found the supplies in stock not very large, but production, despite all difficulties, has increased from April up to the present time and the total amount raised, both anthracite and bituminous, for the period of the present coal year has been considerably in excess of what was raised last year.
The question comes:	If there is any
amount of coal in the United States and the output has increased as compared with last year, why the high prices and why the consequent fears of shortage? There are several principal reasons for it. In the first place there is a vastly increased demand in the United States for industrial and war purposes. The increase of steel which is computed to be necessary this year and which will be forthcoming, calls for an increase of 40,000,000 tons of coal for that special production alone. The cotton textile factories, the munition factories and other industries, stimulated now by war needs, are calling for increased quantities of coal. The railways have to do the hauling and it is computed that the railways this year will require thirty per cent more coal for haulage purposes than they consumed last year, which works out at about an extra amount of 40,000,000 tons or over. That has to be taken into account and it is not possible or probable that the demand will be decreased. In proportion as industry carries on its work of war preparation coal becomes more and more necessary.
One cannot understand the coal situation in the United States, even comparatively, unless he also takes into account the transportation situation which is so intimately connected with the distribution and even the production of coal, as tardy or speedy distribution forms a most important element in coal mining. There has been a comparative shortage of railway transport

for coal purposes. Barges and ships along the Atlantic coast and barges and shipB on the lakes have been transferred in large tonnage quantities from the carriage of coal to the carriage of more remunerative freights. Many of these vessels, both on the lakes and on the Atlantic coast, have been diverted into war activities, either by purchase or by charter. Thus there has been and is a shortage of shipping carriage for coal. With reference to the railways, the demands upon them for the carriage of other freight than coal have been very great. They have not in the United States a co-ordinating body such as our Kailway Commission, but, in order to cope with the situation, some months ago the railroad presidents of the United States met in Washington and voluntarily submitted themselves to the regulative control of a committee of five or six railway men. The American railroads are now administered so far as transport arrangements go, as if all were under one system and managed by this railroad war committee. As a result of their work, voluntary entirely, they have cut out, up to the present, more than 16,000,000 miles of train services and have thus saved thereby 1,120,000 tons of coal, which motive power, man power, and fuel power can now be diverted to more necessary carriage. They have also taken hold of the car distribution and within the last three months have diverted 106,000 empties from railways where they could be spared to railways and districts where they were more necessary and where they could do better service. That shows the improvement that is taking place.
One point to be taken into consideration is that most of the mines in the United States have not storage facilities. They depend upon the coal being carried away as soon as it is raised; and it is the custom of the men in most of the mines, I am told, not to go under ground unless the cars which are to take the product away are there ready for loading; and if the cars are delayed and are not available for loading, no work, or less work, is done in the mines, 'and to a corresponding extent there is disorganization and confusion amongst labour itself. A part of the shortage which has occurred is, of course, due to the transference of alien labourers by hundreds of thousands to European countries to the colours of those countries.
As to what is being done in Canada, the fuel controller and his aides are busy at work on two lines, first to co-ordinate the activities of the dealers and shippers and 
the transport facilities in Canada with a view to equal distribution of the coal when it once arrives at the border, and, second, to look after the supplies that are necessary in the various sections, to ascertain what they are and to make arrangements for their being filled. On the other side of the line the work of the fuel controller and his aide is to keep in co-operative touch with the authorities, the coal miners and operators, the transport facilities and so on, as well as with the Government authorities, to work in touch and unison with them, to get their sympathy and their aid so far as possible. These two lines of their endeavour are being carried on with great pertinacity I know, and I think with very considerable success.
From this short survey of the situation two things are patent as to what Canada will be required to do. It is not impossible, with the wide powers that have been conferred upon the President of the United States and with the work that is being done to ascertain and to regulate the prices and the output, and with the wide powers that we possess to regulate prices and tariffs, that, if activities are maintained as they now are, both the United States and Canada will be, to a certain extent, put upon rations with regard to coal, as distinguishing between absolutely necessary services and services which are not so necessary and which may be dispensed with. In Canada we are taking measure to bring about a complete co-ordination between the different railway companies as to the disposition of cars and the direction of traffic with the view to the saving of coal, just as we are saving in foods. I believe myself that this is absolutely necessary, and that we' can do a great deal in that way.
I have not given to the House particular figures with regard to particular lines that are being followed; it is, perhaps, not best that 1 should. With reference to the lakes, Hon. members will have observed last night that orders have been issued by the Washington authorities to several of the great railway lines to give preference to coal carriage from the mines up to the ports on the lakes so as to provide for the supplies which are necessaries .to go up those lakes during the open navigation season in order to provide for winter necessities.
I have endeavoured to give, as briefly as possible, an idea of the general situation, information which helped me, as I came to understand it, to see the question in its true light, and which may be somewhat helpful to the House.

speechtext: My right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) made no reference to the arrangement which he said some two weeks ago was being made by the Government to place some vessels at the disposition of the authorities in Halifax and St. John, with a view to obtaining ship transportation from the anthracite mines of the United States to those ports. subtopic: COAL SUPPLIES IN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON THE COAL SITUATION.
speechtext:
My statement
still remains true, with some modifications, which it was hinted at the time would be necessary, as to the facilities for unloading large vessels. The fuel controller and his helpers in Halifax and in St. John, had a conference in Montreal, and went over that situation. I think the view is that the transport situation is loosening up considerably with reference to the employment of the smaller vessels, and that there is possibility of getting service at a more reasonable rate. The offer is still open and can be carried out in reference to the larger vessels, to which I referred, in the carrying of large cargoes. The whole matter is under the close advisement of the fuel controller and his helpers in St. John and Halifax, in co-operation with the Department of Marine. Mly hon. friend (Mr Hazen) may have some other knowledge about it.

subtopic: COAL SUPPLIES IN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON THE COAL SITUATION.
speechtext:
HAZEN (Minister of Marine): Some time ago my department took steps to obtain vessels for the carrying of coal from the mines to Halifax and St. John. Great difficulties have been experienced. First of all, we had released, for the Dominion Coal Company, a large ship which had been commandeered during the war by the British Government. We made representation as to the necessity of having that ship in commission for the coal trade. In addition to that, we succeeded in placing' at the disposal of this company vessels which had been commandeered and those vessels have been employed in taking coal to Halifax and St. John, and have relieved the situation, so far as the supply of bituminous coal to these cities is concerned. Some time ago our attention was called to the danger of an anthracite coal famine at St. John, Halifax and other ports, and, on looking into the matter, we found that the
dealers at St. John, Halifax and other places in the Maritime Provinces were justified in exacting the very high prices they charged for coal, in consequence of their being called upon to pay enormous freights for the transport of the coal from New York to points in the Maritime Provinces. The Maritime Province dealers did not purchase from the mines, but purchased generally through dealers in New York, and whereas the carriage of coal before the war cost about $1.50 a ton from New York to points like St. John and Halifax, the schooner owners and vessel owners were now charging as high as $6 a ton, or four times the 'freight charges before the war. In view of this, we notified the fuel controller that the Department of Marine and Fisheries would be prepared, if the dealers obtained the coal for the Maritime ports, to furnish vessels for the purpose of transporting it at what would be regarded, under all circumstances, as a fair and reasonable rate of freight. The vessels that we proposed to place at their disposal were vessels of 3,000 tons. The hard coal which comes to Maritime Province points has not come in large quantities, and it was carried in vessels of 500 or 600 tons or less. The difficulty arose that because the dealers in these places had not facilities for handling great quantities at one time-they had not coal pockets, and storage facilities, for large consignments-it was represented by authorities in St. John and Halifax that, if ships of 3,000 tons were placed at their disposal, it would be impossible for them to handle such large cargoes. The day before yesterday, as stated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, a conference was held in Montreal, at which were present the fuel controller, Mr. Magrath, representatives of the coal interests in Halifax and St. John, and other places in the Maritime Provinces, and the Deputy Minister of Marine. I believe that the general opinion expressed was that there was practically little, if any, danger of a coal famine at any of these ports. It was the consensus of opinion that the matter was largely a schooner proposition, and that the coal must be carried by schooners, and not by the larger vessels. Under these circumstances I have authorized the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries to say to the Fuel Controller that if we are informed that cargoes will be available I will be prepared to recommend the commandeering of schooners to bring that coal to Maritime Province ports at prices considerably less than the prices now charged. It will

be possible to do this, in conjunction with the coal dealers, and if this is done I think it will have the. effect of lessening very materially the prices that are being charged at the present time.

FURTHER CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.	,
The House again in committee on Bill No. 127, the Military Voters' Act, 1917- Hon. Mr. Doherty-Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
On section 6-Information as to the candidates.
What has the minister to say as to my suggestion last night that we should provide for the posting of lists of candidates upon the notice boards of the various battalions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This provision is to
ensure that information as to candidates will reach the different presiding officers at the earliest possible moment. Of course, the purpose of making the provision was that these officers should be in a position to circulate that information so that it might reach the soldiers. I would expect that they would use every means in their power to attain that result. I had it in mind that the details of how they should do that might, perhaps, be dealt with in regulations or instructions under the Act.
I did say last evening-and I am willing

to adhere to it-that, if hon. gentlemen thought it desirable, we could add to this section a provision that the presiding officer should circulate this information by every means at his disposal-or some general words of that kind. We could hardly name in the statute the particular places where he should put the notices up. In the Dominion Elections Act a returning officer is instructed to put up his posters in four of the most prominent places in the district; he is left that much discretion. Perhaps what I have suggested would cover the point raised by my hon. friend.

The minister is always talking about this matter as if mysterious difficulties had to be overcome m order that this information might be conveyed to the soldiers in the camps in England or in France. There is no reason why there should not be a definite statement that publication of these lists shall be made in each of these camps. Under the Dominion Elections Act, a returning officer in Canada must publish notices giving the place of holding the election, the subdivisions of the different ridings where the election is taking place, and the particular places where the polls are to be held.
We have in England 127,000 men, located in the different camps and hospitals. If the minister will look at the military regulations-it is most difficult for hon. gentlemen to get a copy of them-he will see that there are most effectual methods of conveying information to the rank and file. Any one who has ever been through a camp knows that near the adjutant s tent there are a number of bulletin boards on which notices are posted. 'The soldiers make a point of looking for these notices, and in that way any information the commanding officer desires to communicate is quickly disseminated. These bulletin boards are found in every camp in England and France and at the hospitals, and every soldier overseas, except those who are in the front line trenches for a week at a time, or whatever it may be, could be informed of the names of the candidates in that way. Why should we not definitely provide in the statute that the information shall be posted on these boards? Twenty-four hours after our nominations close, the proper officials in England will know the names of every candidate in every constituency in Canada, and the information could be printed and posted up within a further twenty-four hours.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection to putting in as much detail as it is reasonable
to put in a statute, and I have no objection to accepting my hon. friend's suggestion. All I was a little apprehensive of was that if we specified one particular method it might happen that some more effective method of communicating this information to the soldier would be available to the presiding officer, and I had in mind that in the instructions or regulations we should provide that he use every available means of conveying this information. It does seem to me that it would be wiser to adopt that form, rather than to specify one particular method, which, in some instances, perhaps by accident, might not be available.

I think it would be well to follow as closely as possible the method of conveying information that is followed in an ordinary election. Of course, it is not necessary to post up notice of an election in this country, because the people have evidence of its approach practically every night during an election campaign. But around every polling station placards are posted saying where the poll will be held. As the hon. member for Pictou says, in every camp there are bulletin boards, by means of which the commanding officer can convey to every private in the ranks any information he desires to give, and the news is very quickly disseminated. Could not the minister provide in the statute that the information'shall be posted on these boards in the same way that commanding officers furnish other information to the sub-officers and privates, and that where this means is not available some other means shall be adopted? If we leave the door wide open, one presiding officer will use one means of giving the notice and another, another. There would
4 p.m. be no uniformity, with the result, possibly, that a large number of those entitled to vote would not see the notice at all. I think it is preferable that the notice in regard to the election should be posted in the same way that other information is posted for information of the soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The section provides that this information shall be transmitted through all presiding officers. Perhaps we might add to the section something like this :
Presiding officers shall cause placards containing this information to be posted on the bulletin hoards in all camps where the same may be possible, and shall use all other available means of bringing this information to the knowledge of the soldier.

I had in mind something of that nature to be inserted in the instructions. With regard to the requirements in this country, I would point out that the places where this information is to be posted are left to the discretion of the returning officer. Section 88 provides that:
The returning officer shall cause such proclamation to be posted up within the electoral district for which the election is to take place, at four of the most prominent and conspicuous places in each city, town and village, or ward of such city, town or village, when it is subdivided into wards, and at four of the most prominent and conspicuous places in each parish, township or division of parish or township.
I think what I am suggesting now is more definite than that, as it requires that the notice shall be posted on the bulletin boards in all camps, where that is possible, and further than that, that every other reasonably available means be used to bring the information to the knowledge of the soldier. I desire to meet the views of hon. members if possible, but with all respect, I do think that this is a matter that might, perhaps, have been left to the instructions to be given to presiding officers.

We have had the opinion of the hon. member for New Westminster as to what the officers on the other side shall do, and in view of the statements that were made by him, a Government supporter, I do not think the minister can complain against hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. The amendment suggested by the minister seems to cover the ground reasonably well, except that it says: " the bulletin boards in all camps." Now, each battalion or corps has a bulletin board, and unless the minister adds something like this: " the bulletin board of each battalion or corps," the notice might be posted on the bulletin board of one battalion in a camp and the men belonging to other battalions might never hear of it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection to inserting that also. I had used the word in the plural,, and I thought it would cover all the boards in the camp. In the definition section of the Act, "Camp" is made to cover every place Where there is a gathering of soldiers under the command of an officer. It would therefore cover every place where a 'bulletin board might exist.
I have no objection, however, to accepting the suggestion, and I therefore beg to move that section 6 be amended by adding the following words:
Presiding officers shall cause placards containing this information to be posted upon the 
bulletin boards of each battalion in all camps where the same may be possible, and shall use all other reasonably available means to bring such Information to the knowledge of thd military elector.
What is the information?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The list of the nominations made in the different electoral districts.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 7-Nomination and polling days.
Does this mean there shall be no deferred elections in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The intention is there shall be no deferred elections in Canada.
Not even in the county of Chicoutimi?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not even in the county of 'Chicoutimi. I must make one correction to that. We have found that with regard to the Yukon territory it would be impossible to carry this out without making a very undue delay between the issue of the election writ and nomination day, and, therefore, I desire to move an amendment to the section, I have not under my band at the moment the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act which make it clear that this undue delay would be caused if we made the nomination day all through Canada await the time when it would be possible to comply with the present requirements of notice, etc., with regard to the Yukon Territory. I therefore beg to move:
That section 7 be amended by inserting in the third line thereof, after the word "districts" the words "except the Yukon Territory."

Is the minister sure
that the twenty-eighth day might not fall upon a Sunday, or a holiday?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will not fall upon a Sunday unless we fix nomination day upon a Sunday, and I thought perhaps we might be entrusted with having sufficient reverence for the Lord's Day not to fix nomination day on a Sunday. As regards statutory holidays, I also think we might be trusted to so arrange nomination day that the corresponding day in the fourth week thereafter will not be a statutory holiday.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

On section 8-Conduct of polls:

I have not had an opportunity of taking part in the discussion of this Bill, on account of absence; but going over it hurriedly this afternoon, it seems to me that paragraph 5 of section 8 is a very, very serious departure from the recognized principles necessary in holding elections in Canada. I realize that there is some difficulty in applying all the well-recognized principles of holding elections in Canada to elections held in war time, and many of the provisions which are being passed here must be very largely experimental. At the same time it is not right to allow a returning officer-I do not care who he may he or how he is appointed-to carry a polling box or bag around as he wants to, and get the men here and there and allow them to vote without having any person present.
I know that appeals to the Minister of Justice as being an unfair provision. I can quite understand there may be cases where there will be a great deal of difficulty in having a really organized poll, but there can be some machinery provided by which some person representing all the interested parties can be notified of the time and place of the voting. We all know that many people aTe unfair about elections, and there is no use of us shutting our eyes to the fact. - Every man in this House knows that even under the most rigid protection which can be afforded by statutes, you will have unfair practices at elections. As the Bill is, if a man wants to ibe unfair, you simply put the power in his hands. You hand over to an officer who is chosen by the Government-and I notice last night the Minister of Justice held the 'Government was not to throw away their powers of conducting the elections, and I admire him for his honesty, because he has admitted that they are going to run the show.
Hear, hear.

That is what the minister admits. Therefore, if he is going to run the show and is going to appoint political partisans to hold these elections in the army, while I admit that there are a lot of men who would not violate their oaths of office, still we know what is liable to happen. He is liable to get men who will not be as scrupulous as others will be. It is an absolute violation of the principles of decency and honesty to allow a man under any circumstances to go around and take votes under conditions which he might say were all right, but under condition in which there would be no opportunity of having anybody present to watch him. I hope the minister will consider clause 5 very carefully and that he will either eliminate it or throw some protection around it, so that there cannot be any possibility of fraud. Everybody admits that the soldier should have a vote. Yet there should be every precaution taken so that there will not be a feeling in this country that unfair methods are being adopted to secure an advantage for one party as against another.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not desire to contest the proposition that an unscrupulous person could abuse his position. But let us get away from the unscrupulous person for a moment and look at it from the side of the soldier voters. What I had in mind in making that provision was this: Soldiers, at the time that the poll is going to be held, say to-morrow, are ordered into the front line, or into the trenches.

That is only in
France.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It possibly might be a good suggestion to limit it to France. That is the class of soldiers that I had in mind and that is the sort of condition with which a conscientious deputy presiding officer could deal. I have such an abiding faith in human nature that I am loth to believe that our officers over there who will be appointed, although they will be appointed by the Governor in Council, like all officers that ever were appointed in this country, would seek to avail themselves of such a provision in order to fraudulently pass over a vote. I would be quite ready to adopt any wording which will restrict that provision in such a way as to diminish any possibility of fraudulent action in regard to it. I would be sorry J,o sacrifice the provision as a whole because we all know that these voters that we are trying to enable to vote will, in large numbers, do their voting in	the valley of the
shadow of death. Under these conditions I think it	would be Unfortunate, if a soldier goes the day before we had arranged for a formal poll at the place where he is to be, and if he is to face death in the performance of his duty, that he should be absolutely prevented from registering his vote in the event of his never getting back. I would anticipate that there would be agreement perhaps that, if it is a reasonable proceeding to provide an opportunity for him to record his vote, it should be provided. I realize that it does provide

a possibility for fraudulent action if you have an unscrupulous voter and an unscrupulous deputy presiding officer. I would really have been glad if I could have conceived of any provision to meet that condition. I would be glad to accept any suggestion with that end in view.

I can offer my hon.
friend a suggestion right off. There is no reason for a provision of this kind in Canada or England. These are two things that might be eliminated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With regard to England, these men are being constantly taken in drafts. A regiment cannot go and most of the men do not go as units to France but they go in drafts. The presiding officer has fixed his poll in a camp in England, say, for the day after to-morrow, and to-morrow a hurry-up call comes for fifty men to go. Must we say that they will have to vote at a formal poll, of which the scrutineers have been notified so that they may be there to verify their votes?

They could vote in France.
Mr. DOHERTY- That is all very well if they get to France in time.

Nobody crosses to
France who does not go through a period of preparation before going to the trenches and every man who crosses does not go into the trenches. Thousands of men in other corps that are auxiliary to the fighting forces are not called upon to go to the front at all. The men who go to France stay at a base for a period of preparation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is one instance and it may be that that the answer is sufficient. But I understand that men are brought hack to England, many of them wounded and some perhaps in a dying condition. Men in large numbers, unfortunately, are severely wounded. Many of them, no doubt, are in danger of death. Many of them die day after day. What I would like to get at by this provision is to make it possible for the votes of these men, under these conditions and circumstances, to be taken without the formality of a poll.
If that is all the minister wants I think we can arrive at something, that is all I want.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be very glad to get a suggestion from the hon. gentleman.

I am not the minister of elections, but I know something about 
elections in Canada. I presume that the gentlemen who have gone overseas have not ceased to be human beings because they happen to have put on the khaki. The minister seems to balk at the expenditure of a little money in order to take this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

Because I notice that only a very limited number of scrutineers are to have their travelling expenses paid. There is more money being squandered on the Maritime Provinces general staff alone than would provide for a hundred elections in France. They are spending $400,000 on the general staff, and when you add to that separation allowances to their wives and a great army of typewriters, batmen, servants and hangers-on, I am sure you will have $600,000 or. $700,000 that is being paid-I will not say squandered-on the little general staff in the Maritime Provinces. Why cannot the minister spend a little of' this money in order to secure a fair election in France? Why can he not have it arranged in some way? I am not just giving him the wording, but if he would accept the idea I would very soon give him the words. The situation would be met if he would provide that no vote shall take place except in the presence of the scrutineers for both parties.
There must be a scrutineer for each party, whether there are two or three, and if those men should be officials paid by the Government the cost involved would be only a few dollars at the very outside. There is no occasion for a hurry-up call such as my hon. friend describes. While 6uoh a condition of affairs might exist, I think he is magnifying the possibility of it, because men do not leave England on a day's notice, and when they arrive in France they do not go at once to the front, but to a base. The presiding officer should not be allowed to receive a ballot except in the presence of a scrutineer for each party, and then all the ballots taken should be sealed up and 6igned by the scrutineers in such a manner that they could not be tampered with or broken open until the final counting. This could all be done very simply and at a very slight expense. There is no occasion to permit the presiding officer to go behind the barracks, or wherever he finds a man who has a right to vote to receive a ballot, and put- it in a bag and keep the bag open for a month, the ballot not -even being sealed in an envelope. If the minister wants an honest vote, I am pointing out a simple method of greatly

improving the machinery for taking it. Surely he should adopt every safeguard which will tend to convince the people and the soldiers that they are being given an honest opportunity of voting and that when they have voted their votes wih be counted and that everything will be right. I am not going to try to hold up the legislation, but I have not before had an opportunity to express my views. I have suggested concisely what, to my mind, would be the remedy for a great evil. I do not insinuate that all the officers he would appoint would be unfair; in fact I think a very large proportion would be fair, would be on their honour and would respect the honour reposed in them. But still, as it is framed, it leaves the suspicion, it leaves ground for argument all over the country, and if the Bill goes through as it is there will be no weapon in the hands of the opponents of the Government that will be as powerful and as potent as the holding up before an audience the provisions of this Military Votes Bill. I appeal to the minister to take this into consideration and see if we cannot agree on something which will be perfectly fair and will give every soldier an opportunity to cast his vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to making it possible to have a sufficient number of scrutineers, the Bill certainly gives every opportunity. The complaint is that we do not pay the scrutineers. But the scrutineers are similar to those who take part in elections in this country. Here is a Bill which enables each political party to create from among the soldiers who are on the spot as many scrutineers-while they are called deputy scrutineers they have all the powers of scrutineers-as they may think suitable or necessary, and the Bill confers upon the deputy scrutineers all the powers of an agent of a candidate under the Dominion Elections Act. Thus it cannot be suggested that, so far as a multitude of scrutineers is concerned, this Bill does not do everything that can be done. Then we are reduced simply to the question of payment of those deputy scrutineers. As I have said, they will, in the very nature of things, be men on the spot, and why should we provide payment for expenses of gentlemen who will not have to travel? Nobody would suggest that we should remunerate or pay the travelling expenses of scrutineers engaged in elections in Canada. The hon. gentleman overlooks the fact that these scrutineers are not to be sent from Canada to carry on the scrutineering operations. I think that, on reflection, he would not suggest that we would send into the camps a lot of civilians to do this duty.
I would assume that each of the parties, looking after its legitimate interests, would provide a number of scrutineers at each camp, and especially at each base, where there are soldiers gathered.
How will it be possible for soldiers to obtain leave of absence from duty to act as scrutineers in a general election, perhaps for two or three days? They have other duties to perform.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, so far as it may be impossible consistently with their military duties, for these men to perform their duties as scrutineers, I have to admit that they will not be able to do so.

My hon. friend is trying to compare the condition of affairs ill Canada with those in France. He must know that there is a difference. In Canada, if I am running as an opponent of che Government, I have just as much right at a poll as the Government man. I am on the ground, and I can. have my agents, and if I fail to appoint my agents, my friends can appoint them. We know each other, and we know the people, and we have all the machinery for protecting ourselves. But when it comes to the army at the front, it is quite different. It may sound very well to say that they provide scrutineers, but the hon. minister knows that the army is under the control of the Government from the day a man is enlisted until he comes back and is discharged. The Government have every facility in the world in the matter. They have access to all the papers whereas I have not the faintest idea where my electors overseas are located. I suppose I have 1,500 electors from Canada over there. I could not tell to-day where twenty-five of them might happen to be. My opponent has all this information, or he could get it from the Government. He ceuld get the name and number of every one of these soldiers, and he could send them literature and instructions. He could appoint his agents and could be represented by his agents at every camp.

Does my hon. friend
not think that hon. members on that side of the House, and we on this side could be trusted, under ordinary circumstances, in the affairs of life, and in matters of sport, to do the square thing? Why, then, cast a shadow of suspicion and send it through

the country, until the fame of the country fairly stinks in our nostrils? Why can the hon. gentleman not give the Government credit for some common honesty such as you find exhibited, say, in a hockey match?

I think I can trust my hon. friend to be fairly decent in an election. I do not know whether he would trust me or not. I do not know whether it makes very much difference, but if he thinks he can turn me away from my views on the matter by throwing mud
I would trust the hon. gentleman.

Thank you. All this
talk about reverencing the soldier is claptrap. We are willing to give him every respect and give him an honest opportunity to cast his vote, but, for Heaven's sake, quit talkii g nonsense. There never is a time that the word " soldier " is mentioned in the House that somebody does not get up and try to do the highfalutin act, as my hon. friend behind me says-I was going to say the nonsensical act. Treat the soldier as a man, and stop trying to wave the flag; get away from all this nonsense and talk business. I say that we, as an opposition, have no opportunity whatever of reaching these people, and getting our agents and our machinery in motion to run an election. There is no use in denying the fact that a soldier is a human being, just the same as he was when he was a civilian in Canada.
Sober or drunk?

He is a human being
just the same.	~
My hon. friend used to characterize him as "drunk." How does he characterize him now?
It is two years since I answered a question of my hon. friend, or held any communication with him, and I am not going to start it now. There is one man in this House who is beneath contempt.
That is the hon. member from Carleton.
I do not propose to parley with him.
The reports from Fredericton do not go well just now for the other side of the House.

The hon. gentleman can see the difficulty of being represented by scrutineers at all of these places, unless there is some special provision made for it. I am only asking the minister to provide that, wherever a poll is held, a scrutineer for both parties must be present, and not merely a scrutineer for one party. I ask that, because the hon. gentleman can see the almost impossibility of the Opposition candidate being represented, unless there is so'me provision made for an official recognition of the scrutineers. My hon. friend talks about the fairness of this! and says it is all done the same as in Canada, but if he will turn to section 8 he will find that this voting does not take place in the presence of the agent. Section 8 says:
(4) The deputy presiding officer shall permit any scrutineer or deputy scrutineer, or, in the absence of both, any one military elector,' to be present at any poll, and to act thereat as agent on behalf of any party, with the powers of an agent of a candidate at a poll! held under Part III.
If my hon. friend will refer to section 9, as to the manner of voting, he will see that. Subsection (c) provides that the voter shall answer under oath before the deputy presiding officer the questions set forth. Subsection (e) says:
(e) The ballot paper shall be marked in the presence of the deputy presiding officer, but>
in such manner as not to disclose to him or1 to any other person any marking thereon.
The presiding officer in all probability will be the colonel of the regiment, and this soldier is taken in, in the presence of the presiding officer, and must mark his vote in his presense, excepting that the presiding officer will turn his back to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He is holding a poll at which the scrutineers must be present, and have all the rights of representatives of the candidates.
I cannot read that in section 9.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It never occurred to my mind that, having said that these gentlemen might be present, and have all the rights of agents of the candidate, that it would be necessary, at each successive step, to say that they should be present.
I take it for granted they are to be present at the holding of the poll, and we proceed to say what the presiding officer shall do at the holding of the poll. All this time these scrutineers are present, and if there is the slightest doubt about it, I will be happy to repeat it in every section.

Subsection 9 does not bear out the hon. minister's statement. Subsection 3 of section 8 reads:
(3) Where conditions make it reasonably possible, the deputy presiding officer shall give public notice of the time and place of an intended poll, and, in cases of polls to be held! without Canada, a special notice to any per-' son whose appointment as a scrutineer oh deputy scrutineer has been communicated to him, with the request that he so notify.
I should like the minister to tell me how in the world is the Opposition candidate going to. be able to notify the deputy returning officer? How would I know who was going to be the deputy returning officer in a poll in France? I have no means of knowing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman understand that it is a matter of appointing scrutineers to represent a particular candidate?
No, I do not think so. He is to represent the party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All these deputy scrutineers are to be appointed by three scrutineers, who are appointed on the nomination of the leader of the hon. gentleman's party.
I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They could certainly ascertain the whereabouts of men whom they would be willing to trust as scrutineers I wouid suppose that these three scrutineers would familiarize themselves with conditions in England and in France and ascertain where the different groups of men were and where services of deputy scrutineers would be required.

How can they do that?
The voting is to commence the day after nomination.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The provision is that
the voting may begin the day after nomination, but the obligation is imposed upon every presiding officer who holds a poll to give these notices. Though the period in which voting can legally be done extends from the day after nomination until the polling day, the requirements of the statute with regard to the giving of notice must be complied with. It had not entered into my mind that in a place where the giving of notice was possible, a presiding officer wou'd arrange for the holding of a poll the day after nomination so as to make the giving of notice impossible.

Why not strike out the
words " where conditions make it reasonably possible"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would hon. gentlemen desire that, if conditions made it impossible to give notice, the soldiers affected should be deprived of their vote?

I cannot imagine any
condition that would make it impossible. They have twenty-eight days within which to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know what
our respective powers of imagination may be. These men to whom we desire to give the vote are living under conditions where they may be voters to-day and may have gone over the great divide by to-morrow.
That does not apply in Canada or in England.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In Canada or in England the conditions will always make the giving of notice reasonably possible.

Why should thtwhole of the machinery provided by this section be established on the assumption that we are dealing with men who are 'voting in France? Why should not the men who are in Canada vote the same as private citizens dc? Why should not the same thing apply in England? For each battalion of 1,C00 men in England, five polls o'"*ht to be provided, at each of which 200 men could vote, under proper conditions and on a day to be fixed. The only place where you need to provide for special conditions is in France. Why word the provision in such a way that any presiding officer anywhere can dispense with notice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Everywhere in England it will be reasonably possible to do these things, and wherever it is reasonably possible all these things will be done.

Why make any
special rule for England?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have not made any special rule about England; we have made a general rule for everywhere.

My hon. friend or his agent on the other side must appoint deputy presiding officers. Why should there not be a scrutineer for each deputy presiding officer, that scrutineer to be present wherever the deputy presiding officer and his clerk hold a poll or accept a vote? If the minister makes provision to this effect and pays the scrutineers for their services, then you will have an honest poll. When the polling has been finished, all the documents should be sealed up and signed by the deputy presiding officer, his poll clerk and the two scrutineers. These

documents could then be sent on to Paris or London-and there would be no question whatever, of unfairness. My hon. friend would not experience any difficulty in hawing standard scrutineers accompany each presiding officer. I suppose that any one presiding officer will not work mo-re than a day or two, because he will he appointed in respect of a particular place; he will take the vote, and that will he the end o-f his duties. There is no necessity for subsection 5 of this section. My hon. friend talks about the men being taken -away in a hurry; that upon a day set for polling the men might have to be -sent off to the trenches; there might be an emergency. My hon. friend is conjuring up something as a justification for the insertion of this clause in the Bill. He knows that these men do not go to the trenches on ten minutes' notice. A regiment goes into the trenches; the men stay there for a certain number of days and then come back for a number of days' rest. There are twenty-eight days within which the vote may be taken. There is no reason why all these votes cannot be taken at the rest camps in the rear in the piesence of scrutineers. There will be no occasion for the deputy presiding officer taking one, one hundred or one thousand votes in any other than the ordinary way, in the presence of the proper officials and of the scrutineers of both parties. My hon. friend knows also that the men do not go from England to France on a day's notice; they have at least a week's notice. Surely there can be some co-operation and confidences between the commanding officers and the general office in London as to the movements of the troops. The returning officers could be notified as to the movements of a certain corps or unit during the subsequent eight or ten days and the polling could be arranged accordingly. We are not trying to block my hon. friend's Bill; we are trying to make it workable, fair and reasonable, so that the people of the country as well as the soldiers themselves will realize that a fair and honest method of voting has been worked out for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am willing to assume that the statement with which the hon. gentleman concludes- is perfectly true. I have not suggested that in any criticism or suggestion that has been made there wa6 anything but the very best intentions. I might suggest that a little reciprocity on the subject would not do any harm.

However that may be, if the absence of that reciprocity is considered useful, I can stand it. Let us see just exactly where it is that we differ about these different details, and we will take first the question of the selection of scrutineers. The hon. gentleman will agree with me that scrutineers for each party will have to be appointed by that party. Now our law provides for that; it empowers each party, through its three chosen representatives, whose expenses we pay, to -select scrutineers. They have perfect liberty of section. If the hon. gentleman goes with me so far, then the difference between us turns exclusively upon the question whether the Government should provide payment for these scrutineers.
That is one difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is one difference. I do not know whether I made myself clear, but as I understand it, the scrutineers will require to be military electors, unless we are to send in to all these different mi'i-tary camps groups of civilians. We thought that so objectionable that with regard to the election officers themselves we have provided that they shall be military electors. That was also done in the previous Act.

Suppose the Opposition scrutineer should suggest that a certain sergeant should be appointed as scrutineer. Is there anything in this Bill that provides for that sergeant getting leave of absence for the purpose of acting? My hon. friend forgets the fact that he has- all the machinery in his hands, and we have none in ours.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall be glad to try and answer all the different questions, but it is rather disconcerting when one is answering one question to have another one put. I was trying to get down to the successive things on which we differ, and I said that the first thing on which we differed was the question whether the Government should pay these scrutineers. Now, unless we are going to upset very materially military operations, it must be anticipated that just as election officers themselves are military electors, the scrutineers will also be found among the military voters. During the preparation of this Bill it has been impressed upon me from the other side at the instance of military officers, that we should see to it that the officers appointed in connection with this .election should be military men, whether privates or officers. I

think in all reason it must be agreed that the scrutineers will have to be found among the same body from which it has been found necessary to provide that the election officers shall toe selected. If that is true, and they have to be appointed by these chosen representatives of the respective parties, it seems to me that we have done everything that could be done in the way of providing facilities for naming, whether we pay the scrutineers or not. Now what is the advantage in our paying them, unless it is going to be an encouragement to seeking scrutineers in one place who will have to move away to other places to perform their scrutineer duties? I do not think the hon. gentleman himself would anticipate that the military authorities would be willing to consent to that sort of thing.
Why not? That is the very question-this is an election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because, even if this be an election, the proper carrying on of the military operations at the front does seem to me to he more important than this particular election.
A couple of dozen men cannot upset military operations at the front, whpre 100.000 men are employed. It is no use talking nonsense of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The toon, member asks me a question, and when I try to answer him he says it is no use talking. What would he like me to do? If I sat down and was silent he would still complain. I am offering what I believe to be perfectly sound reasons. Of course, his judgment and mine may not agree, because I have not the advantage of possessing 5 p.m. the judgment of the hon. gentleman, and I am limited to offering such observations as in my judgment appear to be well founded and sound. It is a matter of intense humiliation to me that my views do not meet with his approval but hardly a disappointment because I did not anticipate very much else. The hon. gentleman quite understands that we shall not reach any helpful results by this sort of commentary on the observations that are made.
I take it that these men must be military men and it does not seem to me to be more reasonable to suggest that a scrutineer shall be provided from a camp, say in England, to go to France to be scrutineer in another camp, than it would toe to suggest that here at home I should send to Halifax or Vancouver or some other place to find a scrutineer to help me in Ste. Anne's Division. As long as I am paying the expenses myself, and as long as I am dealing with people who' are under no obligation superior to the obligations they may think they are under towards me, I am at perfect liberty to do that if I think proper. But we must always remember that we are carrying on an election among men who have very important duties to perform, and I ask the hon. gentleman himself, is it reasonable to suggest that when in any camp of any importance there are, as there must be, numerous friends and supporters of both parties in this country, we should make a provision in this Bill to make it possible, and even to encourage, one or other of the parties to go looking for scrutineers under conditions which would entail travelling expenses? I really think there is no fair ground for complaint in the fact that conditions are such as to make it necessary for the respective parties to select as their scrutineer people who will be on the ground and who, toeing on the ground, will of necessity not have to go to any expense in the performance of their duties.
Mr. COPtP: How is the candidate going to know where his friends are who will act as scrutineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I thought we all understood that we had not in contemplation the providing of scrutineers to represent particular candidates. I myself, notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman says of the immense opportunities that I have for knowledge of where my electors are, must say that I have never so far been able to find out where particular soldiers were. I have not had occasion to ask for them in connection with an election, but have had occasion to ask for them in connection with other things. Last evening the hon. member for Piictou asked whether we could not lay on the Table samples of lists showing, among other things, the whereabouts of soldiers. I asked the Minister of Militia today whether such lists were available and whether they could be had, and he seemed to be under the belief that there must be some misapprehension with regard to the description of the lists which were referred to. I myself have no knowledge of the existence of such information being available to anybody. But even supposing that the hon. member knew where some of his friends were located, this Bill does not pretend to make a provision whereby it will be possible for him to select a scrutineer for himself, and send hiir, to where his friends are.

Of course he may, if he has that information, communicate with the representatives of his own party who have the nomination of scrutineers, and they will, no doubt, be very glad to meet his suggestion, but the Bill does not undertake to make precise provisions so that every candidate may have scrutineers at the poll. The best we can hope to obtain is adequate provision for representation of the respective parties at the poll.

This poll is to he kept
open continuously from the morning after nomination day until eight o'clock of the day of the election, so that votes may be polled morning, noon or night? There is no intermission at all? They can vote at night as well as they can in the day?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am obliged to my hon. friend for the information; I did not know that.

I ask the Minister of
Justice if it is so?
Mr. DOlHERTY:	The Bill conta ins the
information, and the Bill does not provide for polls being open all day and all night for four weeks.
I simply asked the Minister of Justice for the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And I am giving the
information.
Under the provisions of the Bill, is it not permissible that the poll could be held at night, just as well as in the day-time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is permissible, and
there might be conditions when night would be the most suitable'time for everybody.
I just wanted the information. I was not at all impertinent to the minister; I suppose we are entitled to the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly, and the hon. gentleman has the information now. As I understood his question, he wished to know if the Bill provided that the poll should be open morning, noon, and night for twenty-eight days. I have tried to answer him.

I stated that according
to the wording of the Act, as I understand it, the poll could be kept open morning, noon, and night until eight o'clock of the day of the election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hours at which the poll may be kept open are not prescribed. Within that period they may be kept open

at any time that military exigencies permit. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman would suggest that this should not be done. It seems to me we should leave it possible for polls to be held at such hours as may be most convenient under the particular circumstances as they arise.

In the case of a man who might be on the point of leaving for France, is provision made under subsection 5 of section 8 to prevent him from voting again in France, or voting at two or three different points?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only possible safeguard we have against that, whether a man votes that way or in some other way, is that every voter is required to swear he has not previously voted in the course of the election; just as in this country the only precaution we have against a man voting more than once, if he can succeed in getting by the officers, is his oath that he has not previously voted.

The minister has not yet discussed the proposition I put up to him. Perhaps I may be allowed to place it before him again, and in doing so I wish to quote section 11, although we have not yet reached it, as indicating what I have in my mind. Section 11 at least presumes that a deputy presiding officer may hold more than one poll, or rather he may hold a poll, for instance, for the 25th Regiment to-day, for the 26th to-morrow, and for the 27th the day following. He may travel around from place to place. It also provides that when the bag is full he can seal it up, and start with another one. He does the sealing himself; it is not done by the scrutineer. Why could not the scrutineers appointed by the leader of the Opposition receive notice immediately upon the appointment of the deputy presiding officer that such and such an officer has beep appointed. Then the scrutineer, or scrutineers, could be named to accompany that deputy presiding officer, and wherever the deputy presiding officer accepts a vote the scrutineer would have the right to be present. He would follow the deputy presiding officer around. There should be some direct provision that any man appointed as a scrutineer, or deputy scrutineer, should have leave of absence for the time necessary to attend to the voting. Aly hon. friend points out the difficulty of taking men away from their military duties, and I quite understand that difficulty, but at the same time we must remember this is an extraordinary condition we are providing for the soldiers. We

must realize it is something that will only happen, I hope, once in our lives, therefore we should make a special law to provide for a special case. I have no idea how many deputy presiding officers there might be, but if they are going to travel around and cover extensive territory, there will not he very many of them. If they only take a poll in their own regiment, the amount of time they will require is not considerable, and their pay would be a mere bagatelle. I would like to see a deputy scrutineer for every presiding officer, and I think no ballot should be deposited in the box except in the presence of that deputy scrutineer. If my hon. friend will accept that principle he will eliminate a great deal of discussion in regard to this Act, and he will get his Bill through, because we can easily work out the details. After the ballots have been taken in any particular place I would suggest that those ballots be sealed up in a package, and signed by the returning officer, the poll clerk and the scrutineers in such a way that the seals could not be broken without detection. If the minister will accept that I am sure in a very short time we can arrange for the wording of the changes and the Bill can go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to closing up the box immediately after the ballots have been taken, as compared with the system under which the box is to be finally closed and sealed only after it is full, or after the officer has taken all the ballots he contemplates taking, or it is possible for him to take, I may say these two systems formed the subject of discussion and consideration when we were engaged in preparing the Bill. When we come to the section dealing with that, I shall be glad to put before the committee the reasons which led us to the conclusion that this was the better way. If in the judgment of this committee the method suggested by my hon. friend is considered the better method, I shall be quite prepared to accept it. For the moment we might let that particular phase of the subject stand. With regard to the principle involved in connection with the scrutineers, as I understood it, my hon. friend suggested that every scrutineer should be notified of the names of the presiding officers?
Y:. CARVELL: What I suggested was that the scrutineers for each party-that is, the three scrutineers appointed by the leader of the Government and the three
appointed by the leader of the Opposition- should be notified of the appointment of each deputy presiding officer, then they could arrange for scrutineers to represent each party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I certainly think he ought to have knowledge. When we provided for the appointment of these gentlemen and gave them all the rights of representatives of Canada, it did not suggest itself" to my mind that they would not make inquiry. It must be remembered that the presiding officers named will not be very numerous. I would suppose that a dozen would be more than enough to take care of the work in England and France. I would have assumed that if I had been performing the duty of scrutineer on behalf of my party it would have been part of my business to make inquiry in regard to these deputy presiding officers. However, I have not the slightest objection to making it the duty of the presiding officers, as they appoint ieputy presiding officers, to notify the representatives of each party. I have no objection to adding that provision to the Bill.
Go a little further and provide that no votes can be polled except in the presence of the scrutineers, and then we will eliminate a whole lot of discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I realize that there is force in a great deal of what the hon. gentleman says on the subject, but, on the other hand, I must ask myself: Are we going to create a situation in which the soldier will have to lose his vote because he does not happen to be at a formal poll?
What is the difference between that man and a man in Canada who is a ratepayer and a good citizen and who loses his vote on account of not complying with the conditions of the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The man in Canada is his own master and he has his own time. He may have to make a sacrifice to get to the poll, and if he is ill he may not be able to get to the poll. If he is not detained by superior authority, or if he is not ordered to go elsewhere, he will have an opportunity of polling his vote. Then he is not exposed to the dangers to which the soldier is exposed. I do not want to indulge in any highfalutin, but there are some facts in connection with this matter which are not highfalutin.' Surely it is a more serious matter to say >to a man who is called to go 'away to-morrow to face death.



You cannot vote because the poll is not to be held until the day after to-morrow, than it is to say that to the man at home who is pursuing his ordinary avocation, although I
quite admit that the man. rat home may not live until the day after to-morrow.
He is entitled to his vote just the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Here we have a condition of affairs where it is permissible to vote at any period within four weeks. Here is a man going out and taking the grave chance that he will not come back or that he will come back severely wounded and in very serious danger that he will not live until the day after to-morrow. That condition may exist and it does exist in a large number of cases. If under these circumstances it is possible to have that man's vote taken without undue risk of its giving rise to abuses we should provide means by which it could be taken otherwise than at a formal poll.
I entirely agree with that and I think that probably the minister has shown that there is some difference between the citizen and the ordinary soldier because the soldier is under orders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is that the only difference? Is he not performing a supreme service to the State?

Yes, we admit all that. We admit that the soldier is entitled to vote. We are giving him 28 days to record his vote. The minister states that a man is sent to the front and that he is liable to be killed. Whether he is liable to be killed or not-I do not think there is any argument at all-he is a soldier and therefore entitled to his vote. If the minister would only meet the suggestion he would get rid altogether of the objection. Why not make provision that the presiding officer shall notify the scrutineer because you have got the scrutineers any way?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have pretty well got together so far-
We cannot hear as well as hon. gentlemen opposite can. Would the minister let us know how far he and the hon. gentleman have got together?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have got together to this extent that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) agrees with me that, if it be possible that a soldier's vote could be taken otherwise than at the formal poll under conditions which make it necessary without any undue opportunity for abuse, it would be desirable that the vote should be

so taken. All that is provided in the Bill is that it should be done otherwise than at the formal poll. I am not seeking to conclude from that that I have met the thing upon which we are agreed because I quite understand the suggestion of the hon. member is that, though it might be taken otherwise than at a formal poll, it ought to be required that a scrutineer would be present.
That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And to that end we
ought to make provision for the appointment of sufficient scrutineers. I am quite prepared to supplement the provision for the appointment of a suffic'er t number of scrutineers by imposing expressly upon the presiding officer who names the deputies the obligation of giving notice to the general representative of each party so that the latter may be in a position to know who the deputy presiding officers are and so that they will be in a position to provide a scrutineer for each deputy presiding officer.
One step further; let the deputy presiding officer be required to notify the scrutineer that he is going to accept a vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Now we have reached
the real question as to what is possible. If that is possible, why, of course, it ought to be done. We have already made it the duty of the deputy presiding officer, wherever the conditions make it reasonably possible, to give notice of the poll that he is going to hold. Perhaps, technically, the taking of one vote is the holding of a poll, but I do not suggest that it should be so understood. It seems to me that we have gone as far as we can go when we make it possible for each party to provide that there should be a scrutineer for each deputy presiding officer and have made it the duty of the deputy presiding officer, wherever conditions make it possible, to notify that scrutineer that he is going to take a vote.

You leave a loophole
there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I concede that there i3 a loophole there through which some fraud may come in; but it seems to me that we have to choose between a loophole through which fraud may come and saying to the soldier that under such circumstances he will of a certainty lose his vote.
How will he be deprived of his vote by providing that the scrutineer shall be notified before his vote is taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the conditions that necessitate taking his vote otherwise than at a formal poll arise, say, this morning and the scrutineer has been called away for the day from the camp-
He would appoint some one else in his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will be satisfied with a provision that where-ever it is possible to get the scrutineer-

It is always possible.
Mr. DOHERTY-I think I have gone about as far as I can go to meet the hon. gentleman.

My hon. friend is asking us to legislate for an impossible case. All our men are collected in camps, and when a presiding officer goes to camp to take the votes in it, his scrutineer will be with him in normal cases, and why should he not have him there?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am trying to make
provision for the taking of a vote under conditions that will not occur every day and, with all respect, I do not think it reasonable to suggest that because you have a scrutineer appointed for the deputy presiding officer, that scrutineer will at all times be available. Now it is suggested that somebody else should replace him. I have no objection, in fact the provision for the holding of the poll provides for another military elector acting in the absence of the scrutineer, and I have no objection to make the requirement that wherever that thing could be done it should be done. Hon. gentlemen say there is never going to be a case where that will not be possible.
