Then I am not asking much for the soldier when I ask that that opportunity should be given to him, if the hon. gentleman should happen to be mistaken and such cases should arise.
If a scrutineer has been appointed on each side for each deputy returning officer-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the Dominion Elections Act there is a provision that if there is no authorized representative of either one candidate or the other, electors can come forward and claim the right to act at the opening of the po}l.
That same provision is here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Why could you not provide that if there is no official scrutineer present the deputy returning officer should select two men who should each
represent one side and have the votes taken in that way? I should like my hon. friend to bear in mind that, notwithstanding all he has said, these votes are to be polled under conditions that none of us can realize, not even those who have been at the front.
That would not be so in England.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am speaking of the men at the front and of what the Minister of Justice has in mind, the polling of votes at the front. I should like to impress this: the holding of an election in France and in Great Britain, particularly in France, involves the necessity of most careful provisions, but we must ensure the fullest possible opportunity for voting and at the same time provide adequate safeguards. That is the object of the Dominion Elections Act. That is the object of these provisions, which take into account the holding of an election in a situation that is very difficult and much more complicated than anything we have in this country. I should like to impress upon the committee that we ought to try to make the provisions of the simplest possible character. They will have to be carried out by men whose minds for the most part-I am speaking of those at the front-are intent upon the sternest duty men could be called on to fulfil and who would not have the opportunity to sit down and study these provisions very attentively. Therefore these provisions should be of the simplest possible character. We should avoid complex provisions if we wish to have the election carried out so that men will have a full opportunity to vote and also that no technical questions will be raised with regard to it. It seems to me that the provision I have suggested, which is veTy much like that in the Dominion Elections Act, ought to be reasonably satisfactory. It may be that this provision will never be invoked or, on the contrary, it may be invoked very often; one condition or the other will depend on what is going on at the front, on the developments of warfare which will be taking place when this Act is put into operation. Imagine endeavouring to carry out this Bill in the midst of the awful conflict raging during the last four or five days on the outskirts of the town of Lens! I think any one of us, without exercising his imagination to the full, can realize how intently the minds of all engaged in that struggle would be absorbed in the duties immediately before them, and of how little concern they -would think the strict fulfilment of

techni-oai! provisions of this Bill compared with the sterner duties facing them.

I quite agree with every word the Prime Minister has said, and I do not think that, with twenty-eight days in which to take an election vote, anybody would ever dream of trying to take the ballots of men engaged in a movement such as that around Lens to-day.
If the votes are to (be taken at many different points you must have a returning officer and a clerk, who shall visit each point. I presume a vote would not be taken without the clerk, and why, then, should you not have the scrutineers also? My hon. friend says: " If there is nobody there to represent one party, the returning officer or deputy returning officer can appoint scrutineers. But supposing there is only one man present, how can you have scrutineers to represent a party? My hon. friend is too astute a lawyer not to toe able to understand the proposition that is presented. These scrutineers are to be appointed toy the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition. They are to be notified of the appointment of every deputy presiding officer, and then they have sufficient time in which to nominate a scrutineer for each deputy presiding officer, and the deputy presiding officer shall take votes without notifying the scrutineers. Of course, if he has notified them, and they do not come, it is their fault. That gives the scrutineer the opportunity, if he cannot be present, to appoint a substitute if notice is given. These things will then be worked out, and there will be a feeling that nothing which is unfair or underhand is being done. That is all I ask for. I think we should extend the section to include a private, so that, if necessary, a private could be appointed as a scrutineer. He should have permission to follow the presiding officer wherever he goes, and his travelling expenses should be paid. If you want to appoint a private, then appoint him, and give him leave of absence. No votes should be taken unless the scrutineers on both sides have 'been notified. They could make their own arrangements. If that is done a lot of the discussion will be obviated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We intend to provide that the presiding officer shall be notified of the appointment of the deputy presiding officer. I suggest, in view of what has been said, that the presence of the scrutineer or some representative of the candidate, should be provided for.
Or proof given of his having been notified?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have drafted a proposed amendment that may perhaps be satisfactory, although the words may not be absolutely so. My proposed amendment reads:
But such vote shall he so taken In the presence of the deputy scrutineer, or failing either or both, of a military elector or two military electors, who shall together with the deputy presiding officer sign upon the envelope in which the ballot is inserted a certificate that the vote was taken under this subsection, and the reasons which made it necessary.

There is an obligation upon the Government to provide the necessary machinery to enable the soldiers to record their votes in this election. That, I think, is conceded by all. Beyond question, some soldiers wild foe unable to poll their votes in what is called the formal polls. Shall we give those soldiers no opportunity to poll their votes, or shall we endeavour to provide machinery whereby they may be enabled to do so? In the case of an election in Canada, the Government provides a man who is called the deputy returning officer, and recognizes the appointment of a man who is called a poll clerk. The duties of the poll clerk may be regarded as clerical, but the very fact that he is in the polling booth with the deputy returning officer is, to some extent, a safeguard in respect of the registering of the votes. Moreover, each party may be represented by a scrutineer. If there are two candidates, each has his scrutineer; if there are three candidates, there will be three scrutineers. It has never been regarded as an obligation upon the Government to provide scrutineers for the parties and to pay for their services, but these scrutineers have always been permitted to have a place in the polling booths; they have been recognized to that extent. If we go that far in this case, what fault can be found? The deputy returning officer will go to France or to some other place to take the votes which cannot he polled in the formal booths. The man who should go with him is the man who would be in the booth with him if the vote was taken in

the formal poll-that is, the poll clerk. In sending out those two men to take the vote, the Government is providing the same safeguard that is provided in any election held in Canada. As I understand the Bill, the parties interested may provide scrutineers who may be present when these votes are taken. The member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) says that we should appoint two scrutineers, one to represent the Government and one to represent the Opposition. But does that cover the whole case? So far as this side of the House is concerned, one scrutineer would be sufficient, but would it be fair to appoint only one scrutineer to represent the Opposition? Surely no person would say that. If you represent by accredited scrutineers, paid by the Government, the various elements that constitute the Opposition, you impose upon the Government the necessity of sending with the deputy returning officer a small army of men to see that the vote is properly polled. For instance, there would be one scrutineer to represent the Government side; there would be another scrutineer to represent the Laurier Liberals, another to represent the anti-conscription Liberals and the Bourassa element, and a dozen-
They will be represented by the Government.
And there are the Patenaude Tories and the Paquet Tories.

Hon. gentlemen seem to think that if the Government appointed two scrutineers and paid their travelling expenses, that would meet the case. But in order to represent all the various elements in the Opposition, at least fifteen or twenty scrutineers would be required.
We are satisfied with one; we are not asking for fifteen.
One would be better than none.

If you want one, the machinery is provided here the same as it is in an ordinary election. Any party will have the privilege of sending scrutineers to look after its own interests. The Government send the deputy returning officer and his poll clerk; they provide all the machinery that is provided in an ordinary election and all the usual safeguards. I do not think it is reasonable to ask that they should go further than that.

In an ordinary election, the polling is done at a stated time and place; in this case provision is made that

votes may be taken, not at a stated time and place. That is the difference.

There is another vast difference. If any fraud is committed in connection with an election in Canada, those who commit the frauds can he prosecuted under our criminal law, but I scarcely think our criminal law could reach those who commit frauds in France in connection with the polling of votes.

My right hon. friend
has called attention to the extraordinary conditions which exist in France. I quite admit that the conditions there are extraordinary, but this Bill provides the same machinery, and is equally defective in its safeguards, in respect to elections which may be taken outside of France as in France. The same provision applies to all elections held outside of Canada, wherever they may be held. I am told that conditions in England, so far as the taking of a vote is concerned, are substantially the same as conditions in Canada, and that there would not be the slightest difficulty in taking the vote there.
What about those undergoing medical treatment who are not in bed, but are still not well enough to go to the poll?

Does the minister not think he ought to make provision for two parts in this Bill, one for the men not in France or not near the firing line, and the other for those who are liable to be called to the trenches at any moment? With conditions as they are in Canada, for instance,
I see no reason why the soldiers in Canada could not poll their votes in one day just as the men in a city poll their votes in one day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That provision is in the Act.

Under ordinary conditions, there are a large number of men, and with one deputy returning officer to so many voters the poll should be all taken in one day. I see no reason why the Elections Act as we have it in Canada could not apply to the soldiers' vote being taken in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are some things that would be different-the method of taking the vote, for instance. We have subjected the actual method of marking the ballot by the soldiers in Canada to the rules that prevail here; but we use this form of military ballot, and the reason for so doing is that in taking votes in camps in Canada you would be face to face with the same situation, that you cannot establish separate polls for the different constituencies without very great inconvenience.
That is only in the poll.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is only in the poll. If my memory serves me right, we have, generally speaking, with regard to the provisions for marking the ballot, maintained the requirement that the soldier in Canada shall retire behind a screen to mark his ballot, differing in that from the method provided for overseas voting. As we go along it will be found that there are other material differences. In this Bill we have not made two separate parts, but we have made different provision as to the method of taking the ballots in Canada. Bearing in mind what was said this afternoon, 1 would be disposed to do what I mentioned to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), and that is to impose on the deputy presiding officer, when he takes any vote outside of the formal poll, to insist on taking it in the presence of the scrutineers, or failing that, in presence of a military elector or military electors. I desire to enact
any precaution that can possioly be enacted and for that purpose am willing to provide that with regard to a ballot taken in that exceptional way the presiding officer taking it, and the scrutineers or military electors present, should join in signing the certificate to be endorsed upon the envelope, stating the fact that this particular ballot was taken in this exceptional way, and the reasons why that course was followed. I submit to the committee that with those additional safeguards it is not an unreasonable proposition. And I want to be in this respect, as in all respects, frank with the committee; that particular subsection was the subject of a good deal of discussion, and the conclusion I arrived at as the wisest course to follow was to insert the provision as it stood in the Bill, quite expecting that it would give rise to difference of opinion, and that suggestions would be made looking to a greater protection. I have had the advantage of listening to the suggestions made. At the moment, at all events, I do not feel that I can quite meet them all. But, as I indicated this afternoon, I would be prepared to meet them to the extent of making provision that when the presiding officer, appoints his deputy presiding officers, he should notify the scrutineer or scrutineers of each party of the appointment. In the second place, I would be prepared to add the provision that the military authorities shall, subject to non-interference with the performance of military duty, give every military elector the time and opportunity to vote; and also, subject to the same condition, that they should give to. every military elector who may be named as deputy scrutineer time and opportunity to perform his duty. I would also be prepared to add the further precautions I have mentioned with regard to the taking of this particular kind of vote. I submit that to the committee as the result of the impression made upon my mind by what has been said, and as being what, at the moment, seems to me as far as it is possible to go without running the risk of depriving soldiers of the opportunity which they should have to vote.

I cannot see why any difference should exist between the conditions under which the soldier should vote in Canada and the conditions under which an ordinary individual should vote. I think the Elections Act should apply to every case in Canada, and I do not see why it should not apply to the men in England as well. You have a large number of men together-

not as large as we have in our cities, yet the cities are divided up into-
There are more voters in some camps than there are in some of the cities.

It is only a question of having more polling booths, and more returning officers. None of the reasons which can be brought forward for special arrangements which are necessary at the front-and we all recognize conditions must be exceptional there-can be said to exist in the camps in Canada. I would go further and say that in Canada we ought to have the ordinary ballot, because the soldiers here will know the candidates. There is no reason why they should not.
Every camp probably will contain representatives from twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty different constituencies.
Surely.
They are all mixed up. You would have to have ballots for almost all the constituencies in Canada. That is the outstanding difficulty.

There is a good deal in what my hon. friend says. Perhaps that is a full reply to what I have been saying as to the ballots. It strikes me as a pretty good reason except that if I were in a camp and I came from the riding of South Renfrew I would know where South Renfrew was voting. I think a polling booth for each riding might be provided in the camp.
You might have only one or two voters from each riding.

No one would have so far to go in a Canadian camp as many electors in South Renfrew have to go on polling day. There is another consideration. Men in Canada are not in the position of the men in France, and I see no reason why the men should not be free on polling day for voting purposes. They should not be marched to the polls by their officers and kept under command, but they should go as free electors, every man as good as an officer on that day as far as his vote is concerned.
Is he not?

We seem to be applying to the men in Canada and in England a set of conditions as if they were on strict military service and subject to this condition and that. Particularly in Canada there is 
no reason why the Government should not say that military law for that day shall be in a measure relaxed so that members of a company, or a battalion, will not feel that they are being taken to the polls to vote under their officer. Most men do not like to be driven to the polls, they would rather go themselves. Most soldiers will not like to be formed in regular formation and marched to the polls.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing in this Act that requires them to be.

There is nothing in this Act, but unless there is some provision that the men shall have that day, not the fifteen minutes or half hour to wait until the officer says: "I am ready and I am going to march you to the polls," that will be the result. Give them election day so that no officer can command them to do this or do that. Make them free so that every man will be at liberty to mark his ballot and so that he will feel that he is not in a military camp and not subject to military discipline on that day. In so far as he is an elector he should be free to go to the polls. The ordinary private in a company who de-pendis on hie officer for promotion and everything else, will feel, as long as he is not given freedom to go as a citizen and not a soldier to vote, that he is under some obligation to the commanding officer. The men should be freed entirely from that in Canada. In fact, a good many'of the soldiers in Canada, where they are at a camp near home, might be allowed to go home and vote at their own polls. I am only pointing out what is the feeling of some of the soldiers with whom I havie discussed this matter. It is like men who are dependent for employment on their employer; he would line them up and drive them to the polls. They do not like that; men like to go themselves without any restrictions or orders from anybody. I am not so sure but that the same thing would apply in England as well. But the principal thing that I wanted to draw attention to was that there are two separate conditions. This Bill ought, I repeat, to be in two parts, one part applying to the conditions existing at the front and the other part to wherever there are men in camps. It is no more trouble to take the vote in a camp than it is to take it in the city of Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When we come to deal with the special sections that deal with the things to be done under the Act we will then have an opportunity of considering

what objection there may be to the provisions made and how far it would be possible to assimilate them more closely to the ordinary system. Subsection 1 of section 8 provides that:
Polls shall be held In such camps or other places, in Canada or elsewhere, as shall be assigned to the charge of presiding officers for the purposes of this Part.
I do not think that would be open to objection. Then the rest of the subsection applies to polls held without Canada. Subsection 2 is the one which makes it a duty to allow facilities to the deputy presiding officer and time and opportunity for the soldier to vote. It was to that section that I proposed to add a provision placing the obligation on the military authorities, subject to such action being consistent with the proper performance of military duties, to allow any military scrutineer time and opportunity to perform his duty.
Before six o'clock I asked one question about section 7. I understand that under that section there will be no deferred election in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I moved an amendment this afternoon to except the Yukon Territory where it will be impossible to hold the election because the election list has to be prepared after the issue of the writs. A period of forty days is allowed for it, and if we were to try to bring in the Yukon Territory we would find that it would be impracticable.

Only in two ridings in Quebec, Chicoutimi and Gaspe, have the elections generally been deferred. There is no need now, with the railway in operation, to defer the election in Gaspe, and the election may be held on the same day. In the old days it was not possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As we have four weeks between nomination and election day, I do not think there is any need for deferring the election in any place but the Yukon. If it were not for the long delay in preparing the list in the Yukon, that territory would be included also, but we are forced to make an exception of it.

If it were winter in
Gaspe, you would have to take advantage of the section of the Dominion Elections Act which provides that the proclamation shall be wired, because there is no communication in winter, unless it is fair weather, between the mainland and the Magdalen Islands. But, that would be the only exception.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We went into the provisions of the Act and it seemed fairly clear that, in view of the long interval between nomination and election, there would be no substantial difficulty anywhere except in the Yukon.
If the necessary instructions and information can be transmitted by wire, I do not know why the Yukon should be delayed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The principal reason is that in the Yukon the list is prepared after the issue of the writ for the election, and a period of forty days is allowed for the preparation of that list. The four weeks between nomination and election would not be sufficient for the preparation of the list.
It seemed to us that the balance of convenience was in favour of deferring the election in the Yukon rather than delaying the elections all through Canada or devising a new system for the holding of elections in the Yukon.

Mr. Chairman,
can the hon. minister explain why, under section 7 of the Bill, elections shall be held a month after nomination? What is the reason of that change? Formerly there were only eight intervening days. What are we aiming at?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is to make it possible for the soldiers' votes, specially overseas, to be taken before the polls are closed here in Canada.
It would be undesirable, I understand, that an election should first be held in Canada and the result of that election be given out, and that we should then proceed in Europe to take the votes of the soldiers who, under those circumstances, would vote knowing the result in Canada. If we cannot hold all the elections on the same day the elections at all events will be brought to a close on the s aine day on this side of the ocean as on the other side.

The procedure could be reversed. Nomination day on the other side might be fixed three weeks before. It might be better because in large centres, elections will be awfully expensive. I do not know whether it would be possible or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It would hardly be
desirable that nomination day on the other side should occur three weeks before nomination day in Canada, that candidates

should he nominated overseas and that three weeks after they should be nominated here.

Reverting to the Yukon,
that territory can be reached by wire as quickly as Edmonton, and the different outlying points in the Yukon are at no greater distance from telegraph offices than many points in the prairie provinces or British Columbia. If it were desired to hold all the elections on one day, with an interval of four weeks between nomination and election, I can see no reason, with my knowledge of the Yukon, why the election should not be held there at the same time as in other constituencies. The lists in Alberta and Saskatchewan are prepared exactly as they are in the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The machinery for the holding of the election in the Yukon is especially devised for that territory. Provision is made for the appointment of an enumerator in each polling subdivision to make a list of electors, and thirty days is allowed for the making of the list. All of this has to be completed fifteen days before the polling day. As I said, we decided it was more convenient to defer this election than to delay all the elections in Canada or to make new provisions for all of this procedure in the Yukon.

The condition in regard to the preparation of the lists is, in effect, exactly the same in the Yukon as in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and there is no reason why what is done in Saskatchewan and Alberta in the limit of time permitted by the Act should not be done in the Yukon, the hon. minister rests on the point that it would take a week by mail to reach Dawson. That settles it, but I would think proceedings could be taken on information by wire and, in that case, the work would start at Dawson as quickly as it would at Edmonton. There is no greater area to cover, and no populated points at which it would be necessary to have a polling place at greater distances from railroad communication than in the West Edmonton district. The Vermilion settlement on the Peace river is not less than 250 miles from the nearest rail and telegraph points and there would be no difficulty in meeting the conditions, as far as that point is concerned. I think there would be no difficulty in meeting conditions in the Yukon. I do not wish to press the point, but I have some knowledge of the country and of the conditions the minister speaks of, and I do not wish to have the change he proposes made when I am 
present without my stating the facts, as I understand them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not making a change. I am leaving the law as it was in reference to the Yukon. I am making a change in this way, that we are making the dates in all the other constituencies in Canada coincide. Every reason which has been advanced in favour of a deferred election in the Yukon stands good to-day, as I have endeavoured to point out. Things that have to be done after the issue of the writ necessitate a much later date for nomination in that constituency than in other portions of Canada. In all constituencies in Canada, except the Yukon, there must be eight days' notice of poll, but it is not considered unreasonable that in the Yukon two weeks' notice must be given because you have a large unsettled territory through which the news must be published. Before arriving at a conclusion to except the Yukon from the general rule, I made a careful examination of what the result would be, and it has led me to the conclusion I have stated. I might also observe that this section, providing that all the elections shall be held on the same day and excepting the Yukon, has already been passed.
I thought the hon. gentleman spoke of an amendment providing for postponement in the case of the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, this Bill as originally drawn provided for all the elections being held on the same day, and then different matters were pointed out, and the change was made.
Mr. MURPHY- The hon. gentleman was interrupted when explaining some of the subsections of section 8 and indicating an amendment he proposed to introduce with respect thereto. I would like to add my request to that already made by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) as to the advisability of relaxing military discipline on polling day, with respect to the soldiers who are in camp in Canada. The objection made by my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) as to the difficulty of using the ordinary ballot in these camps in Canada has not, in my judgment, such weight as to preclude the adoption of that ballot, inasmuch as twenty-eight days are to elapse between- nomination and polling day. There would, first of all, be no difficulty on the score of time. As to the other feature of the matter-that there would be in each camp representatives from thirty to forty constituencies

that is a matter

which could be ascertained well in advance of polling day, and suitable arrangements could be made to meet a condition of that kind. Therefore, in my judgment, it would be a decided advantage, first, to relax military discipline on polling day in these camps in Canada, and, second, to provide the soldiers in camps with the ordinary ballot instead of the ballot proposed under this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With regard to the suggestion that we should abolish military discipline for the day-
I said "relax."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I used the word "abolish" because that was the impression I had in my mind. However, I think everybody would agree with me that it would not be advisable to have a day in which there would be thousands of men-

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I have in mind the amendment my hon. friend approved of a couple of years ago, when we were both members of the committee to which the Elections Act was referred, and by which we allowed working men certain hours during the day to vote, so that they would have those hours as of right, and not by favour from their employers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have not specified the number of hours, but we have put upon the military authorities the imperative duty of affording every military elector time and opportunity to vote. Until the hon. gentleman from South Renfrew suggested it, it had not occurred to me that the battalions would be paraded and marched up to vote as battalions. I quite conceive it would not be an impossible thing, but the better convenience would be served by letting each man record his own vote at some reasonable time.
That is my idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no provision requiring them to be paraded. The provision is to compel the officer to allow them time and opportunity to vote. If we were to take a period of two hours, it might, perhaps, be a serious interference with the routine of the battalions, and would not, at all events, be necessary. There are times when we have had camps as large as 30,000. It would be pretty difficult to have 30,000 men vote in two hours. I do not think we could anticipate as many as that. If we have to make a fixed period of time we will allow a great deal more time than would
be considered necessary, rather than run the risk of not allowing quite enough time.
If the individual soldier is to be allowed to go by himseli and vote, ten or fifteen minutes might be ample. I am not a military man, and I do not know to what extent two hours of enforced idleness for one day in a camp would be undesirable, but I fancy it would tbe an unnecessary interference with the conduct of the camp operations, and while I would rather see each man go by himself and vote, still, if a battalion was marched up, and the men allowed to go in one after another and mark their ballots, I cannot quite see how the vote would be influenced.

I leave it to the hon. gentleman. He and I are of the same nationality. If I were a private in a company, and my officer paraded me to go and vote, I would feel that I was under the officer all the time, as I would be. My idea is that, during the time of voting, the private is just as good a man as the officer. He ought to feel he is polling a vote as a citizen, and not that he is subject to the command " Eyes right," or " Eyes front," or subject to any orders at all.
I think that he would feel a greater degree of freedom if he was allowed to go to the poll as a citizen, not under orders. If the officers decided to allow so much time to each battalion for purposes of voting, then the men should be allowed to vote as individuals, not particularly as soldiers. I object to their being marched up to the poll under orders and asked individually to step out of the ranks to vote and then step back again.

Under ordinary circumstances it would not be possible to march a battalion up so that the men might vote. In the first place, in the ordinary poll held in Canada only about 100 or 150 votes could be cast in a day. It would take a considerable length of time to enable all the members of a battalion to vote. Under this Act every soldier has to answer certain questions and to take an oath, the form of which is found on the back of the ballot paper. It would be impossible, therefore, for the officer in command to take that proceeding. The propeT proceeding, I should think, would be to allow certain platoons freedom for the afternoon or for a certain portion of the day, during which period they could do their voting. I think we can trust the officers to see that this is done in a reasonable way. In camps in Canada the military duties are usually

over quite early in the afternoon. Under this Act the polls will be open until 8 p.m.; that would give a great many men an opportunity of voting. I do not see that there would be such difficulty as my hon. friend suggests. .	>

Naturally, an officer is a very superior person on account of his position. Suppose that at 8 a.m. the private is under orders to his officer; if when he comes to cast his vote he is not absolutely released from duty, he feels that he is going to the polls by order. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Arthurs) agrees with me that that difficulty should be obviated. It ought to be made clear in the statute that it is the duty of the officers to allow the soldiers to be released from duty for a certain length of time in order that they may vote. They should vote not as soldiers but as free citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a distinction between a soldier and a free citizen?
I mean, as an elector, not under orders.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We can, if we devote our minds to it, regulate every step that is to be taken on election day by the soldiers and by the officers. I do submit, however, that we might leave something to the common sense of the people concerned, both soldiers and officers.
But you do not leave it to the soldiers. The soldier has no mind of his own unless he is released from duty during the day or at the time of voting.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not so sure that the soldier would resent being marched to the poll for the purpose of casting his vote.
I have seen the soldiers paraded to the paymaster's office. They went in one after the other, and they did not refuse the money because they had been taken there under orders. I would suggest to the member for South Renfrew that perhaps such a proceeding would work out to his own advantage, because the soldiers might be naturally inclined to vote against the authority that subjected them to it.
I would not want that advantage.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Seriously, I want to meet as far as I can any suggestion that may be useful. It has been suggested that we have been somewhat fanciful in respect of the possible difficulties of soldiers on the other side of the ocean voting. Pos-
sibly it is somewhat fanciful to suggest that it would make any difference to the soldier whether he was paraded to the poll or not. Our experienced military friend (Mr. Arthurs) points out the improbability of this happening. I do not think that we are running very great risk of wrong being done to anybody. Whatever the officers do will be done under the eye, as it were, of the public in Canada; they will be subject to criticism if they do not give every man fair opportunity to vote. I really think that we can safely take that risk. If we cannot take it, we shall have to make such detailed provisions in this Act that it will take us a very long time indeed to have it passed.
I think I could put it in two lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
might deal with this particular suggestion in two lines, but if we adopt the principle it will take a good many lines to meet all the suggestions in respect to detail that have been made.

The men who are in the military camps are absolutely under military rule, and unless under this legislation they are relieved from that authority when they come to poll their votes, there is no guarantee that they will be so relieved. My hon. friend does not leave much to the common sense of officials where their duties are prescribed by statute. The privileges that these men will be called upon to exercise on this particular day as citizens of Canada will be more important than the work that the officer might want them to do in the military camps.
It would not be possible to relax discipline and allow all the men off for one day in any military camp. That is absolutely out of the question.
I defer to my hon. friend's view, but I still hold my own. I have been in these military camps; very many men obtain leave of absence.
You suggested that they should all be let off.

I submit that it could be done. I was arguing that the duty appertaining to polling day was paramount to the military duty of that day. It is in the interests of the men themselves that they shall be absolutely free from military control on that occasion; that they shall feel that they are marking their ballots as free citizens of Canada. I am not suggesting

that the officers would try to control their votes; that is not my argument. These men will be voting not as soldiers, but as citizens of this country, with all the interests of Canada at heart. There ought to be a specific provision that they shall be allowed to vote in that way. The minister says that they will be allowed to do that by the officers; then why not set it out specifically in the statute? I have as much confidence in the common sense of the officers as anybody has, but if I were a private in the ranks I would feel that so far as the voting was concerned I was as good a man as the commanding officer, and if I were paraded here or there or anywhere else to vote I should feel that I was being led to the poll.

We have considered this section for quite a long time, and the longer we sit on it the farther we get, apparently, from passing it. I do not think that I have seen any one in the House or out of it who can blow hot and cold more successfully than the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham).
That is quite an art.
A moment ago he said that he objected to soldiers being driven by officers to the polls.
I said paraded. I never used the word "driven."

I do not think there is any difference in view of the way the bon. gentleman said it. However, Hansard will decide. Whatever the hon. gentleman said, he intended to impute improper conduct to the officers of the forces against the soldier. He insinuated that the officer had the soldier under his hand when he should not have. That is an insinuation that I think ought to be resented on the floor of this House on behalf of the officers of this country. The hon. gentleman also said that the privates were dependent on 9 p.m. the officers, and under an obligation to them. I think that also ought to be resented and refuted. Personally, I think that if any officer in any camp in Canada attempted to interfere with the right of our Canadian citizen-soldier to exercise his franchise, instead of the >soldier being driven to the poll, the officer would be driven out of the camp.
That would be mutiny.

I have a higher regard
for the Canadian soldier than to imagine
he would stand for treatment of that kind. The hon. gentleman is simply conjuring up imaginary difficulties. What authority has he for suggesting that any of these things are likely to happen? There, is no foundation for his remarks at all. He is simply supposing that things will happen that never have happened. He is suggesting that the Canadian citizen-soldier is going to be simply a serf under the absolute control of his officers.
I know one soldier who was flogged at Borden.
And that one incident is sufficient basis for my hon. friend to make a wholesale attack upon the officers in our forces.
Nonsense. I did not do/ anything of the kind.

And he suggests that our soldiers would accept servility, and that they would not have the manhood to resent interference with their freedom. He said the men should be freed from that-freed from something they have never been subjected to. In that connection he argued that employers of labour herded their men -another insult to the labouring men of this country. I know that the labouring men of this country will not be herded by their employers, and I put the soldier on an equal plane with the labouring man.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member says "hear, hear ". After saying all these things he says " I have every confidence in the officers ". That is what I call blowing hot and cold with a vengeance. I think the Minister of Justice is to be commended for his patience. If ever a man was patient under insidious attacks and puerile attempts to waste the time of the House, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is that man. I think it is time we made a little progress with this Bill.

I am glad that my hon. friend has had the opportunity of making a real political speech, and I suppose he will now have it distributed amongst the gentlemen in his constituency and elsewhere, and perhaps have it published in the Orange Sentinel.
Not a bad paper.

No, I get it and read it regularly. There is not a man in this House but knows that I said nothing in disparagement of the workingman of Can-

ada. I said that he would resent an employer doing any such thing. Nor did I say anything derogatory of the officers. I made it plain that I did not mean to say the officers would do anything wrong, but that the soldier ought to he free from military control at the time he voted. I submit that that is a fair proposition, which can be discussed without any pyrotechnics, and one which the men in the ranks will agree with; and I know something of their feeling.

I do not know whether the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) was hitting at me or not, and I do not know that I need bother my head much about it anyway. I suppose I am a member of this Parliament, and I am not aware that free speech has been abolished yet. I do not think there has been any undue criticism of this Bill-at least not by me.
This is practically the first time I have spoken on the Bill.

There are some features of this Bill that are certainly very objectionable to me, and I believe they are also objectionable to a great many members on both sides of the House. There are three features to which I object. But before taking them up, I think that when hon. gentlemen make suggestions the Government ought to say either "We will meet you and have this thing arranged if possible," or, "We won't." We should then know where we were at. Taking the points to which I object in the order in which they appear in the Bill, subsection 3 of section 3 provides that a man who was a non-resident of Canada at the time of his enlistment can apply his vote to any constituency he may indicate. That is bad in principle. I am going to take the chance of being called a disloyal citizen by my hon. friend from North Perth or some one else-because whenever we talk about soldiers in this House somebody on the other side tells us we are disloyal-and say that I have very grave doubts whether the people of this country feel that a man who is not a resident of Canada should have the right to vote. Let them call that disloyal if they want to; that is what I say. To my certain knowledge in one regiment in this country to-day there are over 1,000 Americans who do not know anything about our laws and the questions upon which they may be called upon to vote. These men are entitled to the very highest respect for having enlisted, but I am not sure that they 	.
ought to have the vote. But if Parliament decides that they should have the vote, surely they should not have the right to apply their vote in any constituency they please. They ought not to be allowed to play the game as somebody wants them to play it. I do not know to what extent it could be done, but I do know that if any officer were so disposed, this provision might give rise to very grave abuses. I do not want to mention the name of the regiment, but I repeat that in one regiment in Canada to-day there are a thousand Americans, or a thousand in perhaps two regiments, in the same place in Canada. If these men are to be given the right to vote, some provision should be made as to where they shall vote. They should not be allowed to distribute their votes as they see fit.
The second thing to which I object-and I think I am voicing the sentiments of hon. gentlemen around me-is that provision of section 8, which gives an officer the right to poll a vote without an agent or representative of both sides being present when the vote is being polled. I am putting it in pretty broad language, but that is the substance of my objection. This could easily be avoided. A provision could easily be framed to safeguard the secrecy and honesty of the ballot. I admit that holding an election at the front is not like holding an election in Canada. In connection with that, I do not believe that any officer-I do not care who he may be, whether he is the most upright man in the world-should be allowed to carry around with him a bag of votes open to the inspection of himself and anybody else for weeks before it is sealed and sent to its proper destination.
That bag should be sealed up at the close of the polling every day, and either the bag itself should be sealed up by three or four men representing both parties, only to be opened when those same persons or representatives of the same persons are present, or the ballots for the one day's proceedings should be put into a package, sealed up, marked by the different parties and forwarded to destination. That comes under section 11. The third proposition to which I object is the provision that this Bill shall apply to the voting in Canada. I am speaking now to the Minister of Justice, who was a member of the subcommittee, of which my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy), my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrop), my hon. friend from Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. AUGUST 22, 1917
Robidoux), my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) and myself, were members. We went over this thing thoroughly, and I think we gave it as fair consideration as possible. As a result of our deliberations, we worked out a scheme in 1915, which is found in chapter 11 of the statutes of that year. A voters' list was provided for the soldiers in Canada and returning officers were appointed. They were governed by the election laws of Canada. Elections were held the same day as the other elections in Canada, and there was no trouble whatever. Why the Government wants to import an entirely new condition of affairs into the voting in Canada, and give a month's time for the polling of votes, is something I cannot understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend allow me? Under this Bill all the soldiers in Canada are to vote on one day. There will be only one election day. In that respect the present Bill does not differ from the old one. We had some discussion on this question before the hon. gentleman came in, and I pointed out that I thought the greatest substantial difference between the way the votes are taken in Canada with regard to the ordinary individual and the way they will be taken with regard to the soldier in this country consists in the fact that the soldier in this country is to use the form of ballot as provided by this Act. We went over the provisions of the old Act which have been referred to and after careful consideration .and giving the best thought we could give as to how it would work out, we decided-of course may have reached a mistaken conclusion-that the endeavour to provide separate ballot boxes for 100, or 200, or 230 different polls, and to take the vote with the ballots appropriate under the ordinary system of holding of polls by constituencies, would entail a great deal of trouble, and would involve a great deal of confusion, It must also be remembered that under the old Act it was contemplated that all of the votes taken in Canada, as well as those taken on the other side, for a constituency should be so collected as to make it possible to send them to the returning officer in the constituency in which the election was being held, and to have them counted. When we abandoned the idea that it was possible to have the overseas votes assorted and sent in that way to the particular constituencies and counted the same evening, it seemed to us that we had to choose between assimilating the soldiers' vote in a certain
degree without distinction of places, and endeavouring absolutely to assimilate the vote in Canada to the general system of voting. In my judgment, the practical difference, as I have already said, consists only in this, that the ballot is to be the form of the military ballot and to be deposited in the envelopes, and left to be assorted afterwards. I think it can hardly be disputed that it will add a great deal to the convenience of the taking of the votes, if the votes of the soldiers as they present themselves can be taken without distinction between their constituencies, leaving the assortment to take place afterwards and by officers of the same class as is provided with regard to overseas voting, but under the direction of the general returning officer here. It seems to me we get a simpler and more expeditious way of getting the votes taken in the camp, and one which wil-l give rise to less possible confusion, and be likely to create less interruption in the carrying on of the operations of the camp than would be the result if' we have to try to provide separate polling arrangements for every constituency in the Dominion. As regards the method of marking the ballot, the retiring behind the screen and the secrecy of the ballot, we have preserved in Canada the requirements made for the general voting in Canada; and speaking in a general way I do not think there is a material difference between the system of the soldier voting in Canada and the other electors voting, save that the soldier does not vote in a poll set aside for a particular constituency, and does not use the ballot provided for a particular constituency. If my hon. friend had been here this afternoon, he would have heard the discussion that took place with Tegard to the means provided by this Act in order to enable every soldier elector to know the candidates in his particular constituency. I think those provisions are ample. They have been improved by an amendment added at the suggestion of the hon. member for Pietou (Mr. Macdonald), making it quite clear that every soldier shall have ample opportunity of knowing the candidates in his particular constituency, and this Bill affords him perfect opportunity to vote for one or other of those candidates.

Will the minister pardon me? I did not read carefully the provisions of section 7. I see now that the voting in Canada shall all take place on the same day. I am rather inclined to agree with the minister that so far as the actual voting is concerned the provisions of this

Act should prevail, because we could not have, perhaps, a dozen different 'ballot boxes in the same regiment. I am only trying to see if we cannot arrive at some means by which we can shorten this discussion and get the Bill through. So far as I am concerned, I do not like Ottawa sufficiently well to remain here until October 7, if I can help it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps this suggestion might help in attaining the result. We have had a pretty thorough discussion of the sections, as far as we have gone-and I do not by any means wish to suppress further suggestions with regard to them- and I think we shall attain a better result if we let this section stand, and take up the next one, with a view to hearing what may be said on it, then, let that section stand, and so far as suggestions are made the Government would be in a position to take them all together.
I think that is fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We can then see what suggestions can be met, and what suggestions we are not in a position to accept. In that way we would reach a practical result, which, I appreciate, is the wish of every one.

I wish to say a word with regard to section 8 before it stands at the suggestion of the minister. Outside of Canada the only three places in which any number of soldiers' votes will be polled will be England, France and Bermuda. I cannot see why the vote taken in England should not be taken exactly in the same way as it is in Canada. The soldiers in Elngland will not be more considerably distributed than in Canada. They will be held in large numbers in the several camps in different sections of England. There is no reason why all the votes in England should not be polled on the same day.
What about all the hospitals in England in which there will be soldiers?

I do not know why they should not be polled in the hospitals on the same day. I think it would be better to poll them on one day rather than on several days in the hospitals. Surely the hospital officials will not want deputy returning officers coming to the hospitals day after day. In all the training camps in England it would surely be more convenient for the military authorities, and for the soldiers too, that all the votes
	.
should be polled on one day under the protection of the scrutineers. In Bermuda, necessarily, the votes will all be polled on one day. There is no necessity of having different days and this great stretch of time for polling. The only place where this question of mystery, with which the Minister of Justice seems to surround the voting, will have any application will be France. There is only one place in France where the votes can be taken. The soldiers will either be on the firing line, in the four weeks between nomination day and election day, or in the reserve line. The Canadian troops, I would suppose, hold twenty-five or thirty miles of trenches.
Twelve miles.

They hold twelve miles of trenches. During these four weeks the soldiers may be in the trenches, and on the firing line, where no voting can be done, and they can only vote when they return to the rest places or reserves. All these voters in France, or the bulk of them, will be on rest or reserve line extending over a space of about 12 miles. What difficulty is there in having their vote taken on one or two days? Let the returning officer fix the days. Let the scrutineers be present when the ballots are marked and placed in the box, and, when they are placed in the box, let the box be sealed in the same manner as in Canada. I cannot see that there is any difficulty or mystery surrounding this question of the soldiers voting. It looks, from the standpoint of the layman, as if it would be an exceedingly easy matter when it comes down to the mere work of recording the votes.	I am inclined to
insist that the vote should be polled in France on certain days to be fixed by the deputy presiding officers to suit the convenience of the military authorities; that when these votes are polled they shall be polled in the presence of scrutineers, who are there not as scrutineers for candidates but as scrutineers for parties; that in the presence of the scrutineers the ballots shall be marked and placed in envelopes; that the envelopes, at the end of the day, shall be placed in the ballot box; that the ballot box shall be sealed, and that the deputy returning officer shall not be permitted to carry the ballot box around in his possession for a week half full of ballots. Under the section he can open or close the poll when he likes, early in the morning or at midnight, in short, at any hour of the day or night, or at any time to suit the

exigencies of the military authorities. That is bad for the soldiers themselves. The soldiers will have a desire to feel convinced that their ballots have been properly marked, that they will reach the goal for which they are intended, and that the person-Government or Opposition candidate -for whom they have voted will receive the just and true recompense of those votes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. German) has given an illustration of how simple it is for us, comfortably seated in this Chamber, to arrange for the expeditious taking of the votes overseas. My hon. friend says that he speaks at a distance. Well, he does speak at a great distance from the reality. I was in England in 1915.
I had the intention at that time of visiting every Canadian wounded soldier whom 1 could find in the British Islands or in France. There was not anything like the number of wounded then that there is now, and they were scattered from one end of the United Kingdom to the other in 143 different hospitals. That was the condition with regard to the wounded. There were then 143 different hospitals at various places at which the votes of Canadian wounded soldiers would be taken under this Bill. Besides that, there is a new condition in regard to certain arms of the service. Forestry battalions have been scattered over different parts of the United Kingdom, sometimes in small groups. You would find them at many different places. I should have said, in regard to the hospitals, that I obtained a list of the hospitals in which Canadian wounded were to be found. I succeeded in going to something over forty of them in the intervals between my work, but I frequently found this condition: I had a list of the men in a particular hospital, but I would find half or two-thirds of these men there and in the meantime the others had been moved to other hospitals or to convalescent homes. Imagine for one moment the project which my hon. friend seriously puts forward, of trying to take the votes of the wounded in one day. You would require something like 150 or 160 returning officers. According to the argument that was put forward, you would require 300 or 320 scrutineers. The suggestion seems to me to indicate the utter unreality of my hon. friend's project for taking these votes. Besides that, what condition have we in France? My hon. friend tells us seriously that all the Canadian forces in France are concentrated within twelve miles. That indicates an absolute lack of appreciation on his part of the conditions.
I said they were holding that number of miles of trenches.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend forgets that we have forestry battalions and railway construction battalions in France, cavalry units scattered over the country in small groups, fifty or sixty or seventy miles from the trenches held by the Canadians, ready to be brought into action when called for. When I was in France last March we had units of the Canadian forestry battalion carrying on their operations in the Vosges, one hundred or one hundred and fifty miles away from the Canadian trenches, and the Canadian railway construction corps were not near these trenches but far away on the Somme, carrying on operations wherever they would be most useful. If any hon. gentleman imagines that it will be an easy thing, under the simplest possible procedure, to obtain the votes of our forces in. France, while he may be perfectly sincere, it is an indication that he has an absolute lack of appreciation of the conditions in France; he does not understand them. Our forces of different arms are scattered over half of France and it will be a tremendous task to enable those men to have a reasonable opportunity of voting, under the best conditions we can devise. It is most difficult to realize those conditions, and I admit that I have but an imperfect appreciation of them in all probability, although I have been twice in France at the Canadian front. To carry out such a suggestion as my hon. friend offers under the actual conditions at the front would be quite impossible. Then, too, our men in England are in more camps than my hon. friend 'has any idea of.

Last evening I suggested that the Minister of Militia might furnish a statement in fuller form of such information as the Prime Minister has just given, a general statement of the disposition of the Canadian troops in the United Kingdom and in Europe.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will realize at once that it would be absolutely against the public interest that the disposition of the Canadian forces in France should be stated to this committee; it could not be thought of for a moment. So far as Great Britain is concerned, I think there would be no objection to giving details as to the camps, although I should not like to speak positively about that. I omitted to refer to the taking of the votes of the men engaged in patrol service in the North sea, in mine sweeping, and in the Canadian vol-



unteer reserve, scattered among fifteen, twenty or perhaps forty ships, guarding the British Isles and doing patrol service in the North sea. To give these men a reasonable opportunity of exercising their franchise is surrounded with difficulties and perplexities absolutely beyond the imagination of any one who has not known something of the reality. My idea is that while we are bound to surround the taking of the votes with every reasonable safeguard, we ought to make these provisions as simple as possible and to give these men the best opportunity that is available under the law of this country to exercise their franchise. I feel very strongly that the members of the committee will be animated by a desire to do that, and I would like to impress on the committee that it is exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, for us to realize what that task really is.

If there is any military reason why information, of the nature I have suggested should not be given, that is a sufficient answer. But I think that information could be given in a general way which would be of service and would not be objectionable. I quite agree with the Prime Minister that it would be impossible to hold the voting in Great Britain and France on one day. I rose particularly to call the minister's attention to subsection 3 of section 8. The latter part of the section is very indistinct and difficult to undersand. Am I correct in assuming that it requires the deputy returning officer to give notice to every person who is appointed as a scrutineer of the fact of his appointment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. He is to inform the deputy scrutineer when the information that he receives of the appointment has been accompanied by or followed by ? request that he should do so.
If that is the case, why not express it plainly?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought it was expressed plainly, and, with respect, I still think so. I should be glad to make it more plain if any suggestion is made which will help to do so.

Why not say directly that every scrutineer shall have notice of an intended poll? Why require that the deputy presiding officer must have a request that that communication be conveyed to the scrutineer? I was going to suggest that we insert after the word

"notice," in the fourth last line of that section, the words "special notice shall be given of such polls to any person whose appointment as a scrutineer or deputy scrutineer has been communicated to him," and end there. These words "with the request that he so notify" are hardly good drafting, and certainly are not a good way to express the idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If you suppress those words, you make it the duty of every presiding officer, of whom there may be an exceedingly large number over in France, to send a notice to the scrutineer in England that he, the deputy presiding officer, is going to hold a poll. You will make him send a notice to every deputy scrutineer of whose existence he knows, even though he is in a gathering which makes it perfectly clear that only one deputy scrutineer will come to his poll. As stated this afternoon, there will be at least double as many scrutineers as deputy presiding officers. Would it be desirable to say that every deputy presiding officer must notify every scrutineer of whose existence he knows? They cannot all come.
The scrutineer attached to his polling division.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The scrutineer who
wishes to be assigned his poll-that is the purpose. We ask all the scrutineers-who after all, are the representatives of one or other party-to notify the deputy presiding officers that they are the scrutineers and ask to be notified of the intended poll. It is to bring the two together, so that each deputy presiding officer will know which scrutineers wish to go to him. If the hon. gentleman will give me better English, I shall be delighted to put it in, but I want the substance of the section to remain.
No deputy returning officer would be liable to interpret that section the first day he had it before him, and I am satisfied the minister will try #id improve it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought it was all right. I would be very much obliged if the hon. gentleman would suggest an improvement.
Is it intended to mean that the deputy presiding officer shall give the notice to any scrutineer or deputy scrutineer of any intended poll?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The subsection reads:
(3) Where conditions make it reasonably possible, the deputy presiding officer shall give public notice of the time and place of an in-

tended poll, and, in cases of polls to be held, without Canada, a special notice to any person whose appointment as a scrutineer or, deputy scrutineer has been communicated to him, with the request that he so notify.
To me that is perfectly clear, and I do not know how it could be improved. Supposing the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) were the deputy presiding officer, I would say to him: "You shall give notice to any scrutineer whose appointment has been communicated to you, with the request that you so notify."
Why not say: " If requested, a special notice of any intended poll shall be given to any scrutineer or deputy scrutineer?"-then you have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would then have it, just exactly as I have it now. I have not the slightest objection to insert those words.
It would be plainer if you said: " with the request that he be so notified."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The request is that he notify-not that the deputy be notified.

The more I listen to this discussion the more I am convinced that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Halifax is a good one, namely, that this Bill be referred to a special committee, to be threshed out and referred back to the House for one or two days' discussion. It seems to me there are so many technical questions that we cannot follow intelligently the trend of discussion in this committee. As my hon. friend makes a collection of all the suggestions, will he allow me to come back to what I think is one of the most objectionable sections in the Bill, subsection 3 of section 3?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I made this suggestion a little while ago which seemed to be not [DOT]unacceptable:	We have gone over a certain number of sections and some of them have been allowed to stand. This particular section has been fairly exhaustively discussed, and we also have had some discussion on section 3, which section stands and we will have to go back to it-I think it would really make more intelligible to everybody the particular provisions if we allowed this section to stand, and proceeded with the next one, and after we -have discussed it I would be satisfied to let it stand. Such a course might save time later on. We should get a general idea of the whole Bill and the hon. gentlemen will be quite at liberty to come back to section 3 and deal with it further.

I quite agree with the suggestion of the minister as to this section. Subsection 3 says:
Where conditions make it reasonably possible, the deputy presiding officer shall give public notice of the time and place of an intended poll-
And so on. That is sufficiently wide to leave it entirely open, so far as Canada is concerned, to the deputy presiding officer as to whether or not notice should be given of the poll. I think that language should be more definite and certain as far as Canada is concerned, that notice should be given of the intended poll in any case. Then at the end of section 2, in reference to the suggestion of my hon. friend from Carleton this afternoon in regard to scrutineers, I suggest it should be amended by adding the following words:
and shall allow every scrutineer time and opportunity to perform his duties.
I think that the Prime Minister, when he was dealing with what he thought to be the difficulty of holding polls in England, was referring to the exceptional cases. It is true that there are men in the hospitals, but the Overseas Militia Department has a list of the various hospitals in which the men are located, and there is no reason why there should not be a presiding officer at each of the hospitals. If provision were made to this end, the vote could be taken in one day. As to the forestry units, not more than 14,000 men altogether in England and France are engaged in forestry work. The officials at headquarters know where the forestry battalions are and there is no reason why a presiding officer should not take the vote of each forestry battalion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that subsection 2 of section 8 be amended by inserting in line 31 after the word "his" the word "military" and by adding at the ending of the subsection the following words:
and, subject to the same condition, to every military elector who may be appointed ev deputy scrutineer time and opportunity td perform his duties as such.
To meet the suggestion just made, I move to amend subsection 3 of section 8 by inserting at the beginning of the subsection before the word "where" the words "In Canada and," and by inserting after the word "possible" in the first line the words "without Canada." That would make the provision read as follows:
In Canada, and where conditions make it reasonably possible, without Canada, the deputy returning officer shall, etc.

I move, further, to amend subsection 5 by adding to it the following words:
but such vote shall be so taken in the presence of the deputy scrutineers, or failing either or, both, of a military elector or two military electors, who Shall, together with the deputy, presiding officer, sign upon the envelope in, which the ballot is inserted a certificate that the vote was taken under this subsection and. the reasons which made it necessary.
I think that will be recognized as adding some precaution.
Would the minister let that last amendment stand? The section is a rather complicated one, and we should have time to consider the effect of the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My idea was that we should adopt the amendment and let the section as amended stand.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendments agreed to.
Section, as amended, stands.
On section 9-Manner of voting within and without Canada:

I should like to know why such evident precautions are taken to secure the secrecy of the ballot here in Canada, and such evident precautions are taken that there shall be no secrecy in the taking of the ballot elsewhere than in Canada? It is true that paragraph (e) of section 4 provides that six scrutineers shall be appointed, three for each side, and that every scrutineer shall have and may exercise all the rights of a candidate or his representative at any poll. That would mean that they would have a right to be present at the .polling booth, or wherever the vote was taken. Paragraph (e) of subsection 1 of section 9 provides that when it comes to the voting the ballot paper shall be marked in the presence of the deputy presiding officer in such a manner as not to disclose to him or to any other person any marking thereon. Now, what does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection to adding the words: " and the scrutineers," if that be the suggestion.

I would suggest that the ballot be marked in a compartment, just as is done in Canada. Paragraph (b) of subsection 2 provides that the military voter shall proceed into a compartment so arranged that he may be screened from observation and shall there mark his ballot paper. But when it comes to the voter in

France or anywhere else, there is no such provision for secrecy. I think the same precautions should be taken wherever the vote is held. The men could easily go into some compartment. If the vote is taken in the field there will be a tent, or a blanket could be hung up to screen the voter from Observation, and behind that he could mark his ballot. I think the minister ought to be willing to make the provision for secrecy uniform, wherever the vote is taken.

I would suggest that the form of ballot be changed, and that there be simply three blanks, one to contain the words " Liberal candidate," another " Conservative candidate," and another " Independent candidate." There are only two recognized political parties in Canada, the Conservative party and the Liberal party. All other candidates would be classed as Independents. I think that would simplify matters for the soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At present the ballot
papers provide for voters who desire to vote " for the Government," those who desire to vote " for the Opposition," and those who desire to vote for
10 p.m. the " Independent candidate." Last evening we had the suggestion-and I think there was some merit in it-that we should add a blank in the event of there being a Labour candidate. I do not see that there would be any great gain in substituting the words Liberal and Conservative for the words Government and Opposition, because it is not an impossible thing that gentlemen who are Liberals may want to vote for the Government, and gentlemen who are Conservatives may want to vote against it. And after all, the real issue is, shall the Government succeed or shall it be defeated -defeat, of course, meaning that the Opposition wins. Then, of course, we should be leaving out the great Liberal-Conservative party, which is not without existence in this country, some of us are happy to believe. I do not think we should gain anything by the suggested change.

The only point is that
the ordinary elector is more familiar with the words Liberal and Conservative than with the words Government and Opposition.
Mr. GERMAN1: If the hon. gentleman's suggestion is adopted, it will be necessary to have a space on the ballot paper for the Unionist party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is as yet born. However that may be,

with all respect I do not think we should gain very much by making the change. After all, I think most people have a notion whether they are voting for the government or against it, and perhaps as clear a notion as whether they are voting for a Liberal or a Conservative candidate.
I am prepared to consider the suggestion that was made last evening that we should provide a blank in the event of their being a Labour candidate.
Coming to what was said by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) with regard to the provision for secrecy in Canada and the omission of it overseas, the provisions for secrecy in Canada are a reproduction of the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, and the provisions with regard to voting outside of Canada are a reproduction of the provisions of the Act of 1915. There will be places, I have no doubt, where it will be possible to provide for the voter going behind a screen. On the other hand, I certainly think there are places where it will not be convenient to do that.
