They could always hang up a blanket, even if the vote was taken in the open field1.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is perfectly simple if you are in a room or in a camp in Canada. But it has been impressed upon us by people who saw the vote in connection with the Australian election-it was impressed upon us by the representative of Australia on the other side, through the Canadian representative over there-that it was of the greatest possible importance to make the formalities as simple as possible. Time is of some consequence in the taking of these votes, and I put it to the hon. gentleman, is there very much greater danger of the violation of secrecy when a man takes his ballot and marks it at a distance from me where I cannot see how he marks it, than when he marks it behind a screen?

Let us put it as between the officer and the man, and we must not forget that it is the officer who is to hold this election. We know that in the army there must necessarily be a great distinction between the officer and the private. In order to maintain discipline the private must salute the officer, and he is compelled to look upon him as almost a different being altogether. Sometimes I think there is too much of that business. However, the fact remains. Now, under this Bill, when the man comes before the officer to register his vote, the officer, if so disposed, may
say, "The law says that you shall mark your ballot in my presence," and he can make him do it. I am not saying that any large proportion of the officers would do that, but if an officer wanted to do it, here is his authority.
It is true, if the voter happened to be a lawyer and had read this Act, he might say "Yes, Mr. Officer, that is all very nice, but I find by section 4 of this Act the scrutineers have a right to be here."

Where does the hon. gentleman get his authority for the statement that an officer will be present there? As I understand the Act, the deputy presiding officer may be anybody, and I should think on the average of chances in all probability he would be a private from the-ranks.
My hon. friend is not serious in making that statement?

Absolutely serious.
There are many men among the privates there as well educated as my hon. friend, and just as fit to be deputy presiding officers.

My hon. friend is begging the question. He has been an officer, and has been at the front, and he knows there is about as much chance for a private to be a poll clerk, or a deputy presiding officer, as there is for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. We are discussing this thing seriously, and we are trying to find a way out, and to save time, and the minister is meeting us.
There is no use in making absolutely foolish statements.
I agree with my hon. friend entirely; there is no use of any man making foolish statements, therefore he had better keep quiet for a little while.

At the last military election I voted at a British Columbia camp. The returning officer was a private soldier, and his clerk was another private soldier. I was commanding officer when I went there to vote. The private soldier who was the returning officer swore me.
This Government was not running that election.
Oh, oh.

Now I want to come back to what I was discussing with the minister. My hon, friend beside me suggests that he would like to see the poll book with the name of the officer in it. Of course, we

are compelled to take the word of the hon. gentleman, but naturally we would like to see the poll book. However, we will take his word. We do not want to be strictly regular. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is very unnatural.

For the information of
my hon, friend whose mind is so fine, I will give him the name of the presiding officer. It was Pte. Harold E. Sands. The poll was at Vernon, British Columbia.
Mr. 'CARVELL:	That does not convey
very much to us. However, we will look him up. I was pointing out to the minister the fact that clause (e) subsection 1, section 9, provides that the ballot papers shall be marked in the presence of the deputy presiding officer. There is a section in the Bill which provides that the deputy presiding officer shall be a military elector- I think that is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

And, notwithstanding
the theories put forward by hon. gentlemen opposite, we know that in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred, and in fact I might say in one hundred cases out of one hundred, these deputy presiding officers will be officers. I do not think it is right that the private or the non-com. should be compelled to go, possibly, before his own commanding officer, and that there should be a provision in the law by which that commanding officer could say to him:	"You
have to mark your ballot in my presence; true it is, you can turn your back to me when you are marking it. if you wish to do so, but you must mark it in my presence." Let us look at the thing in the ordinary light of common sense. We are all of age, we have all been through elections and we know exactly how these things are arranged and how simply it is to put into effect the system which would provide for the carrying out of the vote in Canada. Simply have the soldier go behind a screen or somewhere where he would he alone, let him mark his ballot there, and then give it to tlie officer. I hope the minister will consider this. I would also recommend paragraph (g) to the attention of the minister. In case the voter is incapacitated by blindness or other cause, the returning officer is to mark the ballot for him. That should he done in the presence of the representative of each party, they are called "scrutineers " in the Bill. I think it will be agreed that there should be some provision to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Pierhaps I was not correct, but my understanding was that having provided that the scrutineer should be entitled to be present at the poll, and enjoy all the rights of representatives at polls in Canada, it was not necessary to repeat it with regard to each operation, but I have no objection to it. It will put the point beyond all doubt.
If you change section 8 I agree with the minister that the change suggested in paragraph (g) of section 9 would necessarily follow.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection whatever to inserting it. It was some Frenchman who said that that which went without saying went all the better for saying. I am quite prepared to make that amendment. As to_ the other amendment, I will consider the suggestions which have been offered. I recollect that at the time of the passing of the Act of 1915 we did pretty thoroughly thresh out the possibility; and I may say I was led to consider it desirable to preserve the present form by the insistent representations that were made to me by officers who were on the other side at the time of the elections that were held oveT there. What was impressed upon me in a general way was the importance of making the operation of the taking of the ballot as simple as was possible, and making it involve as little time as possible. The Australian authorities made certain suggestions to us, some of which had already been in our minds. They impressed upon us in a general way that^we should make the thing so that there should be as few requirements as possible the absence of which might nullify the vote. Looking at it from that point of view, I was led to think that probably there was no substantial danger in connection with the marking of the ballot in this particular way. There may be something in the suggestion that if the presiding officer be a commanding officer over a particular soldier, it may have some effect, but frankly it does net seem to me there is a great deal in the idea that it would necessarily influence the soldier to let the officer see how he is marking the ballot, in the face of a law which expressly prohibits him seeing it, and in face of the fact, which we will now make perfectly clear, that the scrutineers of the respective parties shall be present. Frankly, it was my belief, after I had given it some consideration, that there probably was as great protection for secrecy in this as there would be in the

provision that a man should go behind a blanket and mark his ballot, because if you are dealing with a presiding officer who wants to see the ballot, and is willing to exert what pressure his position as an officer gives him over the voter in order to see how the ballot is marked, I am very much afraid that marking the ballot behind a screen will not prevent him from seeing it. I know the evidence in some election cases goes to show that even with the screen conditions have been so managed that how a man voted has been ascertained. However, I shall be glad to consider the point-or rather to reconsider it, because we did give considerable thought to it in connection with the preparation of the Bill. I want to look at the places where we ought to insert the word "scrutineer."

I am quite sure that every hon. member in this House is just as anxious as the hon. member for Car-leton (Mr. Carvell) that this voting should be secret. At the same time there are many circumstances under which it will be utterly impossible to have any screened portion, even of a tent, for that purpose. If this vote is taken where a great many of the men are in dug-outs, or in confined quarters, it would not be passible to have an arrangement of that kind. In England there is an average of 25,000 wounded Canadian soldiers, many of whom are unable to get up to mark a ballot, and their votes must be taken by some means in the hospitals. Is it fair to deprive these men of the right to vote, simply because they are in the hospitals? The same thing is true in France. There is a great number of men in the hospitals in France, running into many thousands, and it would be utterly impossible to have any screened apartment, or any private place, where they could mark their ballots.
As far as the deputy presiding officer is concerned, I am quite confident that in many cases there will be no difficulty with regard to the question of authority over the voter. I believe that in many cases the deputy presiding officer would be a noncommissioned officer or man. In our army we find that a majority of our common soldiers are pretty well educated, probably as well educated on the average as the officers are. There is another consideration too. It would be very hard to get an officer to take this responsibility. I am quite sure that no battalion commander or major, would take it. If it were taken by any officer he would be one of junior rank and his authority would be limited to the men with whom he was personally acquainted.
Our junior officers, unfortunately, change very quickly, they do not know very many men personally and they do not interfere with any except the members of their several companies. I am quite sure that , no officer having any considerable authority over his men would accept that position.

Would the adjutant
be too busy?
The adjutant is a very busy man. If it were any officer it would be the quartermaster, or the paymaster. The quartermaster sergeant, or an ordinary sergeant, would be the most likely man.

I would like to suggest that clause (e) of subsection 1 of section 9 might start, in general terms, with the language of the Dominion Elections Act. It would be something like this: "The ballot paper shall be marked wherever reasonably possible"-that is the language of the minister-"so that each voter shall be screened from observation." "Screened from observation" are the words used in section 133 of the Dominion Elections Act. Perhaps that suggestion would help the minister.

In connection with the
screening of voters, or asking voters to mark their ballots behind a screen, it does seem to me that it is almost impraetieable. There are large numbers of wounded men in France and England. It is due to these men, who are suffering quite sufficiently from their wounds and their work, that the task of voting should be made as easy for them as possible. To ask that these men be removed behind a screen to vote is to ask something that is impossible. When we remember that we shall have numbers of men suffering from pneumonia and rheumatism, and perhaps thousands from fractured limbs, many recovering from serious operations which possibly have snatched them from the brink of death, to ask that these men be not allowed to viote unless they mark their ballots behind a screen, or unless screens are put around their beds, does seem to me to be asking something that is unreasonable and unnecessary. The duty of this House is to make the voting for the men at the front as easy as possible while protecting it from all possibility of impropriety. Our first duty is to make it easy for the men to cast their ballots. L was struck by another suggestion that was made to-night by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) regarding the distribution of troops. The hon. gentleman made the suggestion that the voting should

take place on one or two days. Troops that may be in, a certain section at one time may be miles away from there shortly after.
In England?
Yes.
Not at all.

The battle of Messines
Ridge took place early in the morning, and hundreds of men who' had been wounded that morning were being carried in motor ambulances across Charing Cross bridge on their way to hospitals in England that night. Hundreds of men are here to-day and miles away to-morrow. It would be absolutely impossible to consider taking the vote on one or two days in view of the wide distribution of the troops. Every facility should be given to the man who is overseas to poll his vote in this election.

I do not know why it is emphasized that we are trying to prevent some soldier from voting. We have heard that suggestion over and over again since three o'clock this afternoon. I cannot understand, the suggestion that any member on this side of the House is trying to prevent any soldier from voting. Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to be using their utmost ingenuity to conjure up some case in which they can show that a man is presented from voting. Does any one think that I want to prevent a man in a hospital from voting simply because I make some inquiry?
If we put into this Act a provision that every man who votes must go behind a screen it would prevent thousands of wounded men fror voting.

Nobody ever proposed
that at all. I was trying to point out that every military voter in Canada was precisely in that condition. The provision applies to soldiers in the hospitals in Canada, and there are thousands in hospitals.
I have seen men carried on stretchers in Canada, and there are hospital trains going through the country from Halifax to Vancouver, flitted up with special beds. There must be hundreds of soldiers in Canada who could not vote if they were compelled to walk behind a screen.
Why not amend both clauses and say " where possible."

Certainly. None of us are trying to keep men from voting. Sub-
section (g) could easily be amended by inserting some such words as " where possible." I am pointing out principles on which the Bill should be drawn and the amendments prepared. Once we agree upon the principles, there will foe no difficulty in choosing the exact language. None of us want to prevent the injured man from voting any more than the man on the firing line. We contend that every secrecy should be thrown around the casting of the ballot. All we want is an honest ballot and with that we shall foe satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that from the outset we have been substantially agreed upon those two principles-that we ought to provide, so far as possible, an opportunity for the soldier to vote, and that we ought to go as far in the direction of surrounding that vote with precautions to prevent abuse or fraud or illegality as is consistent with giving a reasonable opportunity to vote.
That is all we want.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have taken note of the hon. gentlemen's suggestions and shall be glad to consider them. It has been impressed on us that we should make the operation of voting as simple as possible, and should' so arrange it as to take up as little time as possible. I shall be very glad to give consideration to the suggestions made on this section. We might deal for the moment with these amendments so as to get them out of the way. I would reserve the suggestion to make provision that where reasonably possible the elector shall be screened off. Of course, when it is provided that the elector is to go behind a screen, then you make possible the substitution of a marked ballot. Under the system proposed there is no provision for the initialing of the ballot by the presiding officer, or for the other checks against substitution employed in this country. We were acting on the advice of those who had had experience, that we shall leave as little to be done in the way of writing as possible because the conditions at the front make it desirable that the voting be got through as promptly as it reasonably can be. In the second place, I do not think it any reflection upon these gentlemen over there to say that it is well to bear in mind that although we shall have deputy returning officers just as intelligent as there are anywhere, a great many of them will be entirely unfamiliar with this routine, and there will not be a very great opportunity for

instruction. There will he no time for them to study the Election Act or the instructions which have been transmitted to them, and while I do not want to urge that anything that is necessary should be omitted, I am impressed with the idea that, so far as consistent with the fair protection of the secrecy of the ballot, every incidental procedure that can be done away with should be omitted. If we adopt the screen,
I think it necessarily follows that we must adopt the precautions that are provided to Iks carried out in Canadian camps, with regard to the counterfoil, the numbers on them, and the initials on the back by the officers taking the vote. I think there would be serious reasons to apprehend that in the carrying out of those things, there might be many errors, and we might be troubled with questions as to whether certain ballots should be counted or not. The hon. gentleman has pointed out the reasons why this was open to objection. I hope he will think over matters, as I intend to do; but I think we might as well make the amendments agreed upon now.

I was not in the House when the amendments were proposed. Have you a provision for the ballot box being under lock and key, in which box the ballots and envelopes are to be placed, and which must not be opened until opened by the special returning officer? A thought occurs to me along the line of the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton, (Mr. Carvell), that while we are all anxious to give every soldier the opportunity to vote, we must not regard the voting a plaything. There is no advantage in the soldier voting unless his^vote has, in the result of the election, that influence which the vote of every man ought to have, and it will not do to nullify, or to give the opportunity for partisan presiding officers or others to nullify the influence of the vote of the soldier by putting in fraudulent votes, because the result would be just the same as if the honest soldier had not voted at all.. I want to impress upon the minister as strongly as possible that this Bill gives the greatest opportunity for fraud, and those of us who have had anything to do with elections in Canada know that, without the Government being a party to it the men who are acting for the party machine seem to feel that they are justified in resorting to practices exceedingly improper, and doing things which they would not think for a single moment of doing in private life. Why it is I do not know, but that is the case, and that
is why Parliament has tried to throw around elections certain safeguards. That is why I tried to impress upon the minister the desirability of both political parties having a voice in the nomination of the presiding officer. We have appealed to the Government in vain. Under the provisions of this Bill, the presiding officer will know exactly what the voter is doing. Clause (e) subsection 1, section 9, provides that the ballot paper shall be marked in the presence of the deputy presiding officer, but, in such a way that he will not see how it is marked. Those are two contradictory expressions. My hon. friend knows that where a paper is to be signed in the presence of witnesses, it means that the witness is to see the person make the signature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But in this case it must be done in such a manner that where the signature is placed cannot be seen.

Has the voter to turn his back on the presiding officer? The thing is too absurd to consider for a moment. As the section stands, it will mean that in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the presiding officer will know how the ballot is marked. Then, the Bill makes no provision as to the special kind of pencil to be used. The Dominion Elections Act provides that a black pencil must be used, and I think it must be indelible. Under this Bill any kind of pencil can be used. After the papers are in the bag, or unlocked box, they are in the control of people who might erase the pencil mark and put in another. There is absolutely no safeguard whatever in these matters, and I submit it should be the duty of the minister to protect the honest voter in the exercise of his franchise and prevent, if possible, his vote being nullified by fraudulent practices, and this Bill gives every invitation to the deputy presiding officers and those acting with them to resort to such practices.

To my mind, the most
objectionable provisions of this section is that which allows the deputy presiding officer to carry in his possession for a whole week the ballot box unlocked and unfastened in any way, into which from nomination day to tie day of polling these ballots aTe being deposited.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is not this section
that is open to that objection. Some time ago I made a suggestion which I thought everybody accepted, that when we had dealt with a section and such suggestions as we thought desirable had been made, we

might let it stand and proceed to another. The hon. gentleman is beginning to make objection or criticism, or probably leading up to suggestions, -with regard to a subsequent section. Might I ask that this section stand, and we will come to the section to which his observations apply. In that way we can make a little progress.

I assume the minister, having heard the suggestions made by hon. members on this side of the House, will consider them, with a view of redrafting the section and providing the proposed amendments. The hon. member from Perth spoke about the taking of votes, in answer to the hon. member from Carleton. It appears to me that we should in this section make provision for the majority of cases that exist in England, where the voting can be done just as well as in Canada. If we had made such a provision we should have avoided all the discussion we have had about the impossibility of taking the vote of the sick soldier and the vote of the man in the trenches.
A good deal of the extended consideration of the Bill has been occasioned by the fact that many of its provisions deal with exceptional cases rather than with cases where voting could be carried on as simply as it might be carried on in England. I should think that the whole thing might be re-drafted with a view to providing that the men in the camps outside of Canada shall vote as they do in Canada, exceptional provision being made for taking the votes of men in hospitals and in other exceptional circumstances. I suggested last night that my hon. friend make specific mention of a labour candidate; that could be done in clause (d), subsection 1, section 9. In subsection (g) there is no provision for depositing in the ballot box the ballot marked by the presiding officer on behalf of a person incapacitated by blindness or other cause. I would suggest that at the end of subsection (g) the following words be added "and then deposited in the ballot box in the presence of the voter." That would be in accordance with the terms of the Dominion Elections Act. I would suggest also that the minister take into consideration the provision suggested oy thp member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) with a view to designating specifically what is to be used in the marking of the ballots.
I know that it is des'rable to have a simple Act, but the more definite you make the Act the easier will be its execution by those who have not had experience.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall look up the requirement about the kind of pencil. My impression is that there is no special provision as to what kind of pencil shall be used.
A black pencil.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I leave it to hon. gentlemen whether a ballot should be discarded simply because it is marked with a red pencil.

Is provision made for giving the vote to Canadians who are in the Royal Flying Corps or in other branches of the Imperial service? Will the provisions of this Bill apply to Canadians serving in Salonica, Egypt and Mesopotamia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As at present printed, it covers Canadians serving in the Royal Flying Corps. I announced that I proposed to make it cover every Canadian ordinarily resident in Canada who is a member of any Imperial force. The Bill, however, does not provide for the taking of votes in Salonica, Mesopotamia or Egypt-anywhere outside of Europe.	[DOT]
Mr. iCOCKSHUTT: Salonica is in Europe.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was proceeding to
make an explanation with regard to Egypt.
I shall try to learn to be more precise.
There are many Canadians in England and France who are not covered by section 2 of this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We mentioned particularly the corps in the Imperial Forces composed of Canadians who were grouped together, because we thought that we could get their votes. It is not clear that we shall be able to get the votes of those who are not grouped together; nevertheless we propose to make the definition of military voter include every British subject ordinarily resident in Canada who is in any Imperial force whatever or who is serving in any of the Allied forces. We shall not be able to send presiding officers into these forces to look for_the men, but where they are grouped together we shall send presiding officers, subject, of course, to our being permitted to do so by the authorities in those forces.
I move that clause (d), subsection 1, section 9, be amended by inserting after the word " candidates " in line 16 the words " or labour candidate or candidates," by substituting for the word " person " at the end of the sixteenth line and the words " or persons at the beginning of the seven-

teenth line, the words " any candidate or candidates," and by adding at the end of the seventeenth line after the word elected the words " designated by name. It was pointed out by the member for St. John, in connection with the ballot form, that the words " any person " might give a voter the idea that he could vote for any person he liked, without regard to whether he had been nominated as a candidate.
I assume that paragraph (b) will still be open to consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is intended that the section as so amended will stand. I beg to move that clause (e) subsection 1, section 9, be amended by adding after the words "Presiding Officer" in line 20 the words " and Deputy Scrutineers present or military electors acting in their stead."
What is the object of the word "present"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If scrutineers are notified and nobody comes I do not want to make it impossible for the deputy presiding officer to go on and take the vote.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The same words ought to be inserted in this clause after the word "voter," in line 25. The subsection would then read "who shall then and there in the presence of the voter and deputy scrutineers present or military electors acting in their stead."
Would that cover the case of the illiterate man?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was going to make the insertion in. the case of thd illiterate man when we come to that.

Paragraph (f), subsection 1, section 9 provides that the deputy presiding officer may administer to himself the necessary oath. I never heard of such a thing before. It strikes me as anomalous that a man should administer an oath to himself. I think it would be better to have a clerk administer it to him. It would be extraordinary for a man to say to himself "You do swear that you will do so-and-so.** How could you indict a man for perjury on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As far as the proceedings in France are concerned, I do not think we shall be able to indict anybody for perjury anyway. I am not quite certain that it is always essential that some-
11 p.m. body should hand out a Bible and say "Do you swear?" I have
seen a good deal of swearing where the individual took up the Bible and said I do solemnly swear." The provision in paragraph (f) is open to the objection that we have no evidence that the man took the oath except his own certificate that he took it, but we are relying upon that same man's certificate for the oaths of all the other electors.
Would the minister be rather sorry to see that clause in the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I am not sorry to see it there, because after all it is only permissive. I do not know whether this would be considered very grave, but we have not made it imperative that on all occasions there should be a clerk. As this vote is going to be taken, there is no provision for the keeping of a poll book, and though we have provided for a clerk, we have not made his presence essential. The returning officer may be in a position to fill those envelopes himself, and may or may not under given circumstances have a clerk. This was merely to make it possible, if the circumstances arose, that this man should certify to his own oath. Of course, if he has not a clerk, that will end the possibility of the clerk administering the oath.
That is only as to his vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If he has not a clerk, of course that eliminates the possibility of the clerk administering the oath.
Inasmuch as the cleTk is only permissive, could you not meet the condition by inserting the word "have"?

It strikes me as peculiar.
I have seen a great many statutes in reference to oaths, but I have never yet seen a case where Parliament has solemnly declared that man may swear himself.
Does not my suggestion get over the difficulty?
No.
It must be administered by somebody else, of course. In any event it is only permissive.
I would rather see it left out altogether, because it is of no effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps we might let it stand.
The poll clerk or the scrutineer could administer the oath.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will consider the point.
You may depend on it, if he has to swear himself he will put his vote in.
And, he could not be prosecuted for perjury.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I move that clause (g), subsection 1, section 9, be amended by inserting after the word "voter" in line 33 the words "and in presence of the deputy scrutineers present or military electors acting as such." I move also that the same subsection be amended by adding at the end thereof "and deposit such envelope in the ballot box."
Are the words "blindness or other cause" sufficient to cover the case of an illiterate voter who cannot mark his ballot?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I rather think so. I
do not know whether there is anything really gained by mentioning blindness.

I would like to ask a question as to subsection (e), which says "-the voter shall fold the ballot, place it in the envelope, securely close the same, and hand it to the deputy presiding officer." This is practically the same wording as the statute of 1915. Is it the intention that those envelopes will be such as can be sealed?
I do not think there is anything in the Bill describing the envelopes. I presume it is the intention that they shall be sealed, bilt it does not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I am not mistaken there is a provision somewhere in the Bill that the deputy presiding officer shall seal the envelope. It would be somewhat inconvenient to have each of the voters seal his envelope.
I assume the envelope is to be such as can be sealed, but it does not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The intention was that the deputy presiding officer should seal the envelope. I am afraid that has been omitted in the Bill. We will give that point further consideration. In the meantime we might pass on to section 10.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
On section 10-Votes of civilian officials appointed under this Act, Subsection 2- Military elector resident in Canada:

There should be
some limiting words at the end of this section where provision is made to enter [Mr. Doherty. 1
the name upon the poll book. You may have the case of a person who has been across but whose name is already in the voters' list in the district in which he resides. Perhaps the following words might be inserted at the end of the section: " Provided it is not already on the list of voters in the electoral district." There is no necessity of entering his name if it is already on the list.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have a special
provision to prevent a man from voting more than once. Part of the affidavit that he is required to take is that he has not voted.
No, that is not in form D. If his name was on the list in the district in which he formerly resided he might vote as a military elector and then vote again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Bill provides that he shall be required to swear that he has not already voted. The purpose is to provide a method by which a returned soldier, a man who is no longer in the service and who has been honourably discharged, has a vote because of that fact, if our definition of " military voter " be finally adopted. We wanted to provide for the district in which he should be entitled to vote, and it seemed desirable that we should locate him in the district in which he was residing as a returned soldier rather than in the district in which he resided before he enlisted. His quality as military voter entitles him to vote at his actual residence at the time of voting. He is entitled to have a vote as a returned soldier even though under the provincial law he would not find himself on the list. If he finds himself on the list it will be possible to vote either as a military voter or as an ordinary voter.

Does the minister not
think that he could overcome my difficulty by providing in form D that he shall declare that he has not previously voted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

The ordinary oath in
part III would provide for the case if he had polled his vote as a returned soldier and then tried to vote as an ordinary elector.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is in form D that we have to provide for that.
Will it he necessary for the elector to produce his certificate of discharge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The provision requires it and we thought it was not an unfair provision because this man is getting his vote absolutely on the fact that he once was a soldier and has been honourably discharged. He gets that vote in a place where he has no claim to vote on any other ground. I do not think it is unduly hard on him to ask him to produce his certificate of discharge. He has four weeks in which to get it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.
Does the minister not think we have done a good day's work?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I confess I had an ambition to get over all the sections this evening and pass them. I appreciate the cooperation that we have tried to extend to each other this evening, but I think we should all be in a better position to take the matter up to-morrow if we had gone cursorily over these sections.
We should be in a better humour if we went home to bed.
Is there any way by which a candidate, or somebody on his behalf, could get the roll of any battalion that has gone overseas?
I am told they are all printed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There seems to be some misapprehension. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) last evening mentioned some lists and I said I would speak to the Minister of Militia about them. The hon. member spoke of a list which, among other things, would give the present whereabouts of a battalion.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hansard so mentions it.
I did not intend to say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Minister of Militia informs me that it is quite impossible to get those lists. I understand that the nominal roll-s of the battalions as they left Canada may be procured. Tf my hon. friend had in mind the nominal rolls of battalions, or sample rolls, it would be quite possible to get them.
That would be some help. I suppose the rolls are not complete?

Speaking of the nominal rolls, we have them in the Patriotic Fund. They are only printed up to
the 150th battalion and there are not more than half of them procurable. The rolls for the later drafts are not procurable.

I have in my office rolls of battalions to the number of something like 105 or 110. These rolls were printed as the battalions left Canada and were sent in by the paymaster. These were sent to me, I do not know for what reason.
I received them long before the recess.
There are fully one hundred battalions ot which the rolls are not printed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understood last evening that the hon. member for Halifax desired only to have sample lists.
No, we should like to have the actual rolls.
Yes, it was the lists that we wanted, of each battalion, where they are available.
We all have soldiers in different battalions, and if we had the rolls of the units in which our soldiers are serving we could easily figure out which of our electors were in different units.

Only last week a list of the nominal rolls that are printed was sent out, so that the Militia Department have that information and could easily furnish it.
On section 11-Forwarding the ballots:

Does the minister not think it would be a good idea to carry out the suggestion made by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and that at the close of each day the ballot boxes should be safely sealed and despatched to their destinations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We considered that, but I shall be glad to reconsider it. The reason we abandoned the course now suggested, which would in many ways appear to be the preferable course, was that it would necessitate the employment of a great number of boxes, -with consequently greater difficulty in transporting them and greater work for the officers who attend to the counting. However, I shall be glad to reconsider the suggestion that it would be better, even at the risk of a multiplication of boxes, to provide that each box should be sealed after being used. I quite recognize the desirability of having a more specific provision defining the nature of the ballot box, and I think we would meet the situation if

we put in a provision making it quite clear that section 122, part 3, should apply. I propose that section 122 of the Dominion Elections Act shall apply. That section reads:
The ballot boxes shall be made of some durable material, with one lock and key, and a slit or narrow opening in the top, and so constructed that the ballot papers may be introduced therein, but cannot be withdrawn therefrom unless the box is unlocked.
I think we cover that by our definition that the word "box" shall include any receptacle. That would meet the criticism. I think the word "box" is used here, but we could amend our interpretation section so that a bag might be used and meet the requirements. In the practical operation of other elections that have been held, it has been found that, for the purpose of the election so held, a bag was a more convenient thing for use under conditions in the field than such a metal box. I do not think any one can attach serious importance to the question whether a bag or box is provided, because a bag or box would meet the requirements of section 122. If provision were made that wt, should have a receptacle from which the ballots could not be withdrawn once they were dropped in, and which was securely locked and closed, perhaps that would diminish, to some extent -at all events, the objections made to the deputy presiding officer carrying the bag, or using the same bag on more than one occasion. However, I am glad to consider the suggestion that he should send this back after each operation. What is present to my mind is that we might make provision such as I have suggested applicable to places where you hold something that is really in the nature of a poll and make some exception in cases where the officer may have to go from one group to another, or one hospital to another for the purpose of collecting the ballots of very small collected groups.
I hope the minister will adhere to the box.

I think, under the conditions at the front, it would be impossible to have ballot boxes. The transport is taxed to its limit to carry food and ammunition to the front, and it would be looked upon by the military authorities as an outrage, if yon asked that the same transport should carry a load of empty boxes, when it should be filled with shells. When the ballot is enclosed in an envelope, nobody can find out how a soldier voted, unless he

tampers with that envelope. There is nc reason why the ordinary mail bag, which is capable of	being	well	lockedat night' and kept	in	a	safe	place,should not be used	as	a	baPot box.It will not take up	any	space.	There
are hundreds of bags going up to the line every day, and hundreds of ihem coming back empty. There is no reason why the post office should not supply good mail bags for this purpose. I desire to point- out to hon. gentlemen opposite and to those who have been taking objections and suggesting that there may be irregularities, that the men at the front are not that kind of breed. As a matter of fact, they do not care very much how elections go. They are risking a great deal now, and I would be quite willing to take their method of carrying on the election, without an Act at all. There is no method of posting the names of the candidates on a board. There are no boards over there. All the information is sent to the front by a small telegraph wire.
That is at the front.

Yes, and that is virtually the rule. I do not think the same necessity arises, as in an ordinary election, for ballot boxes. I think Parliament can safely trust the soldiers at the front to see that this vote is fairly taken, and if we cast ourselves on their hands I do not think Parliament will regret it. The crook, the ballot box stuffer and the election thug will not be there. These men are not of that quality. Why all this fuss and all this attempt to establish safeguards? To my mind it is not necessary at all. The point that was raised the other night by the hon. member for Pictou, about the way votes were taken in England, does not apply to this election at all. I think it would be out of the question to send ballot boxes to the front. The proper way would be to put the ballots in a mailbag. That is all you can get over there. They could not understand the necessity for a ballot box. It is absolutely necessary for the transport to handle food and munitions, and every inch of space is required for that service.

I made a suggestion, which 1 still think is worth considering. I realize the difficulty of handling boxes. I have never been there, but one's imagination does not have to go very far in order to appreciate the difficulty. I suggest that, at the close of the polling every day, these sealed envelopes should be taken out, in the

presence of the scrutineers, and put in a sealed package, and marked by the returning officer, his clerk and the scrutineers. That sealed package would be ready to be forwarded to Paris, or London, and the same bag or box is available for the next day.
That is what I had in my mind.

You could preserve the
ballot dox.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: One advantage of the ballot box is that once a ballot is dropped in, it stays there until it gets to the returning officer. By the method suggested by the hon. member for Carleton we lose that. On the other hand, you gain in this way, that you send your ballots off at once. But you have to allow some operation to take place of handling the ballots outside of the presence of the voters and scrutineers between the time that the ballot is deposited and the time that the proper officer counts it.
The safest thing is the bag properly sealed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We might, as I say, make the provision suggested this afternoon -that, at the end of every polling operation, the bag should be sealed up and sent at once; but we might perhaps modify that, so as to make provision for the exceptional case, where one polling operation might be the gathering of four or five votes in a hospital by an officer who would have the time and opportunity to do it, and perhaps he would gather in other groups of the same kind.
You might make some arrangement like that.
Why should these provisions apply to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not see any reason why we should not use the ordinary ballot box in Canada. I was suggesting that we make section 122, which defines the form of ballot box, apply. The section of the Dominion Elections Act which tells us about the form of the ballot box merely provides that the material shall be durable, that it shall have one lock and key and a slit so constructed that the ballot papers may be introduced therein, but cannot be withdrawn therefrom unless the box is unlocked. A leather bag, for instance, could be of durable material; it could have one lock and key, and it could meet with the rest of those requirements.

When a box is used it may be locked during all the time that the ballots are being put into it. The ballots cannot be extracted without unlocking the box. You have to keep a bag, however, open all the time, until all the ballots have been put in.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What applied to the locked box applies also to the locked bag; you can put your envelope into the bag without unlocking it. Why should the bag be open? If you have a bag which conforms to the requirements of section 122, you can put your envelope in through the slit; it will not be necessary to unlock the bag or keep it unlocked.
It is rather inconvenient to have a slit in a bag.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A tin box would not be procurable on the fields of Flanders. They used the bag on the other side, and I do not see any reason-
Why not use a wooden box? That is what we use in New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That goes to indicate that the statute does not require any sacramental thing at all.

The Dominion Government has not any ballot boxes of its own; they always fall back upon the township or municipality for boxes with which to carry on the election. It is time that the Government obtained suitable galvanized boxes, or boxes of some kind, in which the voters could deposit their 'ballots. In one case where an election was held close to the time when a municipal election was also being held, there was a wild scurry to get half a dozen ballot boxes in which to receive the ballots. They had to go to Toronto and take them from the cellars there. I hope that when the Dominion election comes along, ballot boxes will be provided, with safety locks that cannot be opened and without any false compartments. I do not see any reason why the soldier's ballot should not be deposited in its envelope with the other ballots in the ordinary ballot box. When the returning officer comes to open the box and to count the ballots in the presence of the scrutineers, he can place in a sealed envelope the ballot of each soldier cast for a certain riding and send it to the returning officer for that riding. Or he can count the soldiers' ballots then and there and transmit the count to the returning officers of the respective ridings for which the ballots are cast.

Mr. GRAHAM That might be done in Canada.

Yes. In France the objection to providing boxes is very great. Metal or wooden boxes would not get within a mile of the trenches. As for wooden boxes, the fellows would use them to start fires with, because wood is valuable out there; the men carry it round in their pockets to make fires with which to boil their tea kettles. If metal boxes were used, complaint would be made that so much useful steel was used for that purpose when it might more appropriately be shot across at Fritz. The best thing to use would be the standard mail bag. When it is pretty well filled, it could be locked in the presence of the scrutineer and handed over to the brigade post office as registered mail. These votes will have to be taken in brigade areas.
Would it not be advisable to use a smaller bag than the standard' mail bag?
I would send no bag there at all except a bag that would be used in carrying supplies to the district concerned. When it is being sent back, let it carry the ballots.
And let the deputy presiding officer use his coat pocket in the meantime.
I would as soon trust the deputy presiding officer's coat pocket in France as I would the ballot box in New Brunswick.

It is now midnight; we have worked pretty well to-day. I think that we all have a desire to report this Bill and to put it in proper shape as rapidly as possible. Does the minister not think that we had better adjourn?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I accept my hon. friend's suggestion-if hon. gentlemen will promise to be as good to-morrow as they have been this evening.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House adjourned at 12, midnight.
Thursday, August 23, 1917.
